15wv9p5.text: At some point your security will fail. This isn’t pessimism. It’s not because your team and tools aren’t sophisticated enough. It’s the reason we have detections in the first place. And, it’s why once we accept that prevention has its limits, we arrive at an interdiction strategy: finding and disrupting what got in. After the alert The alert tells you something happened. However, gaining access to your network doesn’t necessarily mean attackers have stolen data or disrupted the systems they were targeting. They may need to obtain additional access, move to another machine, or further explore the network. Being able to see and understand that activity is the intervention opportunity. People naturally gravitate toward detections during product evaluations. They’re tangible, easy to compare and quantify, and address the question everyone wants an answer to: Will they catch the attack? There’s often an assumption that the rest will follow, meaning, if the detections are good, surely the investigation will be as well, right? Whether you can trace the attack, understand the scope, and respond in time to intervene depends largely on the data behind that detection. In network security, a product can have good detections and still leave an analyst struggling to investigate. Perhaps the analyst can see the connection that triggered the alert but can’t follow what happened next. If a search returns nothing, does that mean the activity didn’t happen or that you weren’t collecting the evidence needed to see it? This, and the arrival of AI defense, is why data quality has recently been getting so much attention. Data vs. data Investigation success takes knowledge of both attacker behavior and your own environment. You need to understand what you’re looking for, but also what your data can actually tell you. The difference in network data shows up when investigating an alert. Both shallow and rich data provide investigations with a starting point, but one can rapidly lead to a dead end. Shallow data is often just composed of timestamps, IPs, and basic connection information. Rich data retains greater transaction details and adds context. It correlates and lets you pivot and reconstruct, answering not just what triggered the alert but what happened before, after, and elsewhere. To evaluate the data quality of a security tool, consider key questions such as: Are full transaction details provided or just a summary?Is packet content or file extraction available?How far back can we search, and how fast?Can I follow a connection across hosts and time? AI <3 data AI-powered SOC tools can now process data at a scale that human teams simply cannot match. The more data points AI has, the more effectively it can surface events. While shallow data limits what AI can correlate, richer data allows it to identify subtle patterns across hosts and behaviors, potentially exposing previously unseen indicators of compromise or providing opportunity to intervene before an attack escalates. AI can help when something unfamiliar is encountered. Nobody knows every service, process, or log format. An assistant can help explain what you’re looking at, suggest questions to pursue, or write a script to make a large set of data easier to examine. That can save a lot of research time. It can also help an analyst get past a point where they would otherwise be stuck. But we’re certainly not at the point where we can trust what AI claims 100% of the time. You still need to test what it gives you. If an assistant suggests an explanation, check whether the evidence supports it. If it produces a query or script, test what it does. And before running a suggested command, ask what else it might affect. A model can be so focused on solving the immediate problem that it overlooks the rest of the system. As AI takes on more investigative work, the ability to inspect the underlying evidence becomes another essential aspect of modern data quality. Unfamiliar territory is the test When evaluating data from network security products—NDR in particular—take an alert from a demonstration and investigate it properly. But don’t follow the guided path. Dig deep and put yourself in unfamiliar territory. You’ll get a much better sense of how the product helps analysts when they’re dealing with an event they haven’t seen before. Look at the transactions behind the alertAsk what packet content or extracted files are availableFollow the activity backwards and forwards in timeAsk a question that wasn’t anticipated These questions and tasks probably won’t be part of a typical demo. That’s the point. They’ll let you see if the data provides the fidelity, reach, and context to actually solve investigations or just a starting point with nowhere to go. Detections get the attention, but data determines the outcome. The real question is can your team use the data to fully understand an incident and decide what to do? Corelight’s structured network evidence preserves protocol-level context to produce a more complete dataset for investigation and AI. When analysts and AI can reason from evidence instead of isolated alerts or metadata, they can validate findings, reconstruct activity, and reach more reliable conclusions. 1ycxb7y.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined. As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix. The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected. The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27. The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960. Which Updates Carry the Fixes Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update. The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes. The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away. The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component. All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do. Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

1k1kg97.text: Cybersecurity company Barracuda Networks warned that attackers have begun exploiting two recently patched Email Security Gateway (ESG) vulnerabilities that let them run commands with root privileges. Barracuda released security updates to address the two flaws (tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560) one week ago. The first stems from an Email Security Gateway (ESG) authentication weakness that can be exploited to modify an appliance's global configuration, while the second lets unauthenticated attackers inject OS commands that execute with root privileges. Barracuda also said that successful attacks require access to the administrative user interface (Admin UI) of targeted devices and advised customers to restrict access to trusted internal networks and use appropriate network access controls to limit exposure. "Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device," the company explained. On Monday evening, Barracuda updated the initial advisory to warn admins that the two flaws are being exploited in attacks targeting a limited number of customers. "Barracuda immediately initiated a comprehensive remediation process and released security patches for affected products. We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations," it warned. "If a patch has not been automatically applied, customers should manually apply the appropriate patch as soon as possible. If customers have turned off automatic patching, Barracuda recommends setting devices to automatically receive patches." The table embedded below lists all affected devices and available security patches. Affected Product CVE-2026-116606 CVE-2026-111560 Patch Email Security Gateway (ESG) Yes Yes BNSF-40425 (9.4.017+), BNSF-40430 (<9.4.017) Load Balancer ADC No Yes BNADC-16586 Message Archiver (BMA) No Yes BNMA-32468 WAF Control Center (WCC) No Yes BNWF-60060 Web Application Firewall (WAF) No Yes BNADC-16586 Web Security Gateway (WSG) No Yes BNYF-24789 Three years ago, Barracuda patched another Email Security Gateway flaw (CVE-2023-7102) that the UNC4841 hacking group exploited in zero-day attacks to execute arbitrary code. The same year, UNC4841 abused another zero-day (CVE-2023-2868) to target Barracuda ESG appliances as part of a series of cyber-espionage attacks. The company later revealed that the flaw had been exploited as a zero-day for at least seven months, since at least October 2022, to drop previously unknown SeaSpy and Saltwater malware and steal data from compromised devices. According to cybersecurity firm Mandiant, almost a third of systems breached in the 2023 campaign belonged to government agencies, most of them hacked between October and December 2022. Barracuda was founded in 2003 and now has more than 200,000 customers worldwide, including small- to medium-sized businesses (SMBs), large enterprises, and managed service providers (MSPs). 1wdf40n.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Cyber Espionage / Malware The Russia-aligned state-sponsored threat actor known as Turla (aka Snake) is wielding a previously undocumented cyber espionage toolset called Cereal that's used to break into victims' Microsoft Exchange servers with an aim to surreptitiously collect emails. According to an ESET report shared with The Hacker News ahead of publication, the sophisticated and modular tool is designed for long-term intelligence gathering and has been observed against two governmental entities in Kazakhstan and Romania in late 2025. "The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyber espionage," the Slovakian cybersecurity company said. "It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes." "The Cereal toolset demonstrates that, for Turla, Exchange servers are not just mail servers – they are durable collection points, internal execution hubs, and a suitable environment for hiding sophisticated .NET tradecraft." The toolset is a collection of interconnected components that are capable of running on Microsoft Exchange servers, receiving commands, executing them in memory, mapping the infected network, and harvesting emails of interest. The initial access vector used to deliver the malware is unknown, although the group is known to conduct spear-phishing, watering hole, and ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) attacks. Cereal gets its name from the fact that the tools make extensive use of serialization, which refers to the process of converting a data structure or an object's state into a format that can be easily stored, transmitted, and reconstructed. A number of aspects make the malware stand apart - Absence of an external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, instead abusing a compromised Exchange server for this purpose. Sending commands in the form of separate, compiled .NET programs. Using an automated email collection module, which is injected into legitimate Microsoft Exchange processes and is engineered to manipulate the email transport pipeline. The combination of these techniques shows that the threat actor possesses a deep understanding of the internal workings of Microsoft Exchange, ESET added. The Cereal framework consists of eight moving parts that work together to provide the attackers with access to sensitive email data - CerealRunner, which is deployed by the operator and serves as a pathway for dropping additional components, including CerealLoader, CerealSprinter, CerealIron, and CerealMoth. CerealLoader, which loads and runs a .NET assembly from an encrypted file on disk, leading to the execution of CerealSprinter. CerealSprinter, which functions similarly to CerealRunner and is used to decrypt and run CerealNeuron, CerealHermit, and CerealBox. CerealIron, an injector that makes it possible to load and run .NET assemblies from non .NET processes. CerealMoth, which receives an assembly and a method name as inputs, loads the assembly, and runs the specified method. CerealNeuron, a passive backdoor that runs on a compromised Exchange Server and listens for incoming web requests on paths that appear like regular Exchange traffic to execute assemblies contained in CerealRunner binaries. CerealHermit, a variant of CerealNeuron that reads commands from encrypted files on disk and has no network functionality of its own. CerealBox, which is the email harvesting module that processes, filters, and collects email messages by injecting itself into the Exchange transport service ("EdgeTransport.exe"). Upon gaining visibility into the email flow, the malware looks for messages containing DOC, DOCX, or PDF attachments, and matches at least one of many hard-coded lists with sender addresses, recipient addresses, subject lines, or attachment names. Emails that meet the filtering criteria are compressed, encrypted, and staged in files on disk, after which they are exfiltrated and deleted via CerealNeuron commands. In the attack aimed at the Romanian government organization, CerealBox is said to have been configured to gather emails involving NATO and European Union institutional addresses, a pattern that aligns with Russia's strategic priorities. The commands delivered as compiled .NET programs are handled by CerealRunner, which unpacks and executes the payloads in memory and then sends the results back to CerealNeuron for subsequent exfiltration to the threat actor in encrypted format. The commands support retrieving mailboxes or specific messages; queuing Active Directory for computers, users, groups, and DNS records; running Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) queries; extracting LSA Secrets; listing volume snapshots; and performing file operations. "The sheer volume of near-identical binaries, each compiled for a specific task, strongly suggests that the operators have an internal framework that automates the compilation and packaging of commands," ESET researcher Matías Porolli said. "Combined with a codebase built around modular, interchangeable components, the impression is one of a mature, well-engineered platform – rather than a loose collection of scripts."

mkh2fy.text: The Russian state-backed threat group Turla has been using a new malicious toolset called 'Cereal' to intercept emails on Microsoft Exchange servers at government organizations. Researchers at cybersecurity company ESET documented the attacks in late 2025, initially finding modular .NET malware for Microsoft Exchange at a government body in Kazakhstan. A month later, ESET found the same toolset at a government agency in Romania, where it selectively gathered email correspondence with representatives of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and the European Union (EU). "After fine-tuning our detections, we found the same toolset at a governmental organization in Romania - compromised on December 23rd, 2025," the researchers say in a report today. Turla, also known as Snake, Secret Blizzard, and Waterbug, is a cyber-espionage group active for more than two decades and linked to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). In the campaign analyzed by ESET, the hackers use the Cereal toolset, and specifically a component in the kit named CerealBox, to inject into Exchange’s EdgeTransport.exe process and hijack existing transport agents’ handlers. The malware executes commands in memory and can inspect email content without registering a new transport agent or interrupting normal email delivery in the Exchange server. Turla configured the malware to selectively collect messages containing document attachments such as .DOC, .DOCX, and .PDF files, and match certain sender, recipient, and subject criteria. Another malware component, called CerealNeuron, awaits for incoming encrypted web requests on paths resembling legitimate Exchange services, which carry commands for execution. CerealNeuron checks and decrypts the request, then executes the supplied CerealRunner program, a wrapper program that carries the code the attackers want to execute. Attack overview Source: ESET Commands may include code to retrieve emails from Exchange, query Active Directory for users, groups, and DNS records, extract locally stored credentials, read files, or delete files. “The sheer volume of near-identical binaries, each compiled for a specific task, strongly suggests that the operators have an internal framework that automates the compilation and packaging of commands,” ESET says about the disposable programs serving as command carriers. “Combined with a codebase built around modular, interchangeable components, the impression is one of a mature, well-engineered platform – rather than a loose collection of scripts.” The CerealRunner components contain encrypted .NET programs and the arguments needed to run them, which execute in the host’s memory and then return their output to CerealNeuron. Eventually, CerealNeuron encrypts the output and sends it back to the attackers. Command execution flow Source: ESET ESET observed no external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used in the attack, leaving the compromised Exchange server itself to serve as the only control point. The researchers also uncovered a variant of CerealNeuron called CerealHermit, which lacks network capabilities and instead reads commands from encrypted files on the disk. CerealHermit may serve as a fallback/redundancy system for when Neuron’s web channel becomes unavailable. However, ESET didn’t explain how attackers place Hermit’s command files on the server or retrieve the execution results. The researchers note that Cereal’s advanced concealment methods demonstrate Turla’s deep understanding of .NET execution techniques, including abusing the .NET native image cache to run inside legitimate processes. ESET says the Cereal toolset was designed for "long-term, stealthy cyberespionage," featuring a small disk footprint and relying on infrastructure that is less likely to be detected and blocked. The company has shared an extended list of indicators of compromise (IoCs) on its GitHub page. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. keytmj.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Four flaws that attackers could exploit without logging in were fixed today as part of SAP's monthly Security Patch Day—the vendor rates all four 10.0, the maximum CVSS score. Three are in the SAP NetWeaver application server, the software SAP systems run on, and one is in the Web Dispatcher, which receives web requests from the internet and passes them on to that server. The flaws in the Web Dispatcher and the Internet Communication Manager (ICM), which handles the server's web traffic, could allow an attacker who can reach the software over the network to run code, the vendor says. The flaw in the server's SAML 2.0 service provider, which hands off user sign-in to an identity provider, could allow an attacker to log in as any user on some systems that use SAML single sign-on. The flaw in SAP Gateway, which connects the server to other SAP systems and programs, could allow an attacker to impersonate one of the system's own servers and take unauthorized actions. None of the four require any user action to work. Affected Versions and SAP Notes Each flaw is fixed in its own note, and the affected versions differ by component, according to SAP's November security bulletin. The notes are in SAP for Me, which requires a sign-in, and the vendor strongly recommends applying them as a priority. CVE Component SAP Note Affected versions CVE-2026-76964 Internet Communication Manager (ICM), SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP Note 3778530 KRNL64UC 7.53, KERNEL 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, 9.20 CVE-2026-89126 SAP Web Dispatcher Note 3778556 HDB 2.00, KRNL64UC 7.53, WEBDISP 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, XS_ADVANCED_RUNTIME 1.00, SAP_EXTENDED_APP_SERVICES 1, KERNEL 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, 9.20 CVE-2026-89103 SAP Gateway Note 3798345 KRNL64NUC 7.22, 7.22EXT, KRNL64UC 7.22, 7.22EXT, 7.53, 8.04, KERNEL 7.22, 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 8.04, 9.16, 9.20, 9.21 CVE-2026-120017 SAML2 service provider, SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform Note 3849308 SAP_BASIS 702, 731, 740, 750, 751, 752, 753, 754, 755, 756, 757, 758, 816, 920, 921, 922 What Each Flaw Allows On the affected SAML setups, an attacker could use CVE-2026-120017 to log in as privileged users too, according to the vendor. A full compromise could follow, possibly reaching connected systems. A different SAML flaw in the same software, CVE-2026-44748, was fixed on June 9 and needed an attacker with a normal user account. In the ICM flaw (CVE-2026-76964) and the Web Dispatcher flaw (CVE-2026-89126), crafted network traffic could corrupt memory. An attacker who succeeds could then run code and fully compromise the system. SAP Gateway uses access control lists to decide which outside programs may connect to it and which programs it may start. In CVE-2026-89103, the gateway enables its default list with high privileges, allowing an external attacker to be treated as one of the system's own application servers. That attacker could then take unauthorized actions in the application environment. What to Do In its Patch Day analysis, RedRays, a company that reviewed the notes in SAP for Me today, advises updating the kernel and all Web Dispatchers in a single rollout. That rollout should reach levels that cover all 17 of this month's kernel and Web Dispatcher fixes. The firm's guidance for each flaw: SAML2 (CVE-2026-120017). Under certain configurations, the service provider did not check signatures on incoming assertions. Treat any AS ABAP system that uses SAML2 for browser logon, such as Fiori Launchpad or Web GUI behind an identity provider, as in scope until shown otherwise. There is no workaround, so the correction instructions or the listed support package are the only fix. The firm's SAML2 analysis also suggests reviewing every trusted identity provider in transaction SAML2 and checking audit logs for SAML logons by privileged users from unexpected sources. SAP Gateway (CVE-2026-89103). Where secinfo and reginfo hold no explicit rules, or rely on the internal host keyword, the gateway falls back to rules that allow the system's own application servers. An attacker who passes as one of them could then reach the usual gateway attack paths toward command execution. The note lists no workaround. For kernels up to 7.77, the fix adds the profile parameter gw/acl_mode_proxy, which tightens the default rules, while kernels from 7.93 on already have it. The firm's Gateway analysis advises setting it after patching and checking that gw/acl_mode is 1, that secinfo and reginfo hold explicit rules, and that the gateway port (33xx) cannot be reached from user networks or the internet. ICM (CVE-2026-76964). WebSocket control frames with invalid length fields cause a heap out-of-bounds write before any login. SAP NetWeaver AS Java is not affected, and the fix ships through dw.sar and the SP Stack Kernel. If users reach the ICM only through a Web Dispatcher, patching that Web Dispatcher to the levels in FAQ note 3778788 shields the ICM for now, according to the firm's ICM analysis. That holds only if nobody can reach the ICM ports directly. Turning off WebSocket support blocks the bug as a last resort, but it breaks features that depend on it. Web Dispatcher (CVE-2026-89126). It has the same root cause as the ICM flaw. It affects standalone and embedded Web Dispatchers, including those in SAP HANA XS Classic and XS Advanced, but not SAP Content Server. The firm's Web Dispatcher analysis lists the patch paths: SAPWEBDISP.SAR for standalone instances, dw.sar or the SP Stack Kernel for embedded ones, SPS08 revision 089.05 or SPS07 revision 079.11 for HANA XS Classic, and version 1.5.4 or later for XS Advanced. Turning off WebSocket support works until the patch is in, but the note warns that this affects ABAP Push Channels and some Fiori features. Find every Web Dispatcher first, because one missed instance leaves the flaw open.

l5yu54.text: An October cyberattack on refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites was carried out by a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the French government said yesterday. The attackers broke into controllers on the night of October 11 and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. That caused food losses and, in at least 15 cases, fires. The unit is called Shahid Kaveh. It is known mainly through hacktivist personas, such as CyberAveng3rs and Cyber Isnaad Front, that publicly claim some of its attacks, France says. France's Foreign Ministry plans to summon Iran's ambassador and to ask its European partners to adopt new sanctions against Iranian organizations and individuals involved in the attack. The Paris prosecutor's office opened a judicial investigation yesterday against the unit's head, the head's two deputies and anyone else identified. It has asked for international arrest warrants. The offenses under investigation include illegally interfering with computer systems and causing damage by means dangerous to people, both made more serious by the aim of serving a foreign power, Iran. In the October attack, the attackers took remote control of Danfoss and Dixell refrigeration controllers through web interfaces, the prosecutor's office said in a press release. They started abnormal defrost cycles with no time limit and switched off the temperature probes' safety alerts, which should go off above a certain temperature. The attack caused about 20 fires. Most of the organizations hit were large retailers, according to a joint report by France's cyber crisis coordination center, known as C4. They include Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché. Small butcher shops, a slaughterhouse and cooperative food plants were also among the victims. The center also tied the attack to the simultaneous targeting of Schneider Electric equipment at several small hydroelectric installations in France. The effects on that equipment were moderate. In its attribution statement, the ministry estimated the food losses at several tens of millions of euros and called the operation the first offensive cyber campaign on French soil carried out purely for sabotage. How France Tied the Attack to Iran The C4 brings together France's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI), the DGSE and DGSI security services, the armament directorate and the cyber defense command. It says four indicators point to the IRGC as the sponsor of the attack and to Shahid Kaveh as the unit that carried it out. The infrastructure used in the attack was also used during the same period for reconnaissance of Schneider Electric equipment. That equipment is installed at sites such as small- and medium-sized energy and water production sites. The reconnaissance relied on techniques that Shahid Kaveh has used since at least April. The attackers also used FOFA, a scanning tool they usually use. CyberbanNews, a propaganda outlet linked to the unit, reported on the attack as early as October 13. The attack infrastructure also held traces of Persian. Prosecutors said the criminal investigation, run by France's anti-cybercrime office (OFAC) and the DGSI, found an attack method typical of the unit. It also found the use of Persian and IP addresses leading to devices located in Iran. Shahid Kaveh has previously claimed attacks on industrial equipment, according to C4. Through CyberAveng3rs, it claimed an earlier campaign against Unitronics, an Israeli company that makes industrial control systems, in November 2023. In March and April, it claimed a large sabotage campaign against Israeli and U.S. interests that hit industrial control equipment, including Israeli refrigeration equipment. France's attribution does not mention the new wave of refrigeration attacks that struck supermarkets in several other European countries last week. What Operators Should Do France's CERT-FR said in an incident alert that it was aware of numerous compromises affecting remote refrigeration controllers across four product families. They are the Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series, the Copeland xweb, and the Dixell xweb. The alert, last updated on October 16, warned that attack campaigns against this equipment were probably still underway, and that exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice. For controllers that are not compromised, the alert's steps are: Remove internet exposure from these units and from any unit reachable at a public IP address. Check insurance contract terms before cutting off the data feed to the refrigeration contractor. Review the full configuration, especially the defrost ranges. Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. In an emergency, filtering the contractors' IP addresses at a firewall is possible, but it is not a lasting fix. Follow the maker's recommended practices. For Danfoss devices, this includes updating firmware, setting the security level to Strict, and ensuring default passwords have been changed. For compromised controllers, the steps are: Remove internet exposure and check insurance terms, as above. Restart Danfoss equipment, or otherwise restore the device to its factory settings. Restore access only through a secure VPN or a protected network. As above, firewall filtering of contractors' IP addresses is an emergency option, not a lasting fix. Reconfigure the device before putting it back into service, then follow the maker's recommended practices. An end-of-life (EOL) device that receives no security fixes faces a very high risk of compromise if it remains exposed to the internet, the alert warns. In that case, a factory reset alone is not enough: it removes the attackers' persistence, but the device stays vulnerable and will almost certainly be compromised again.

1seityj.text: Google has released emergency security updates to patch a new Chrome vulnerability exploited in zero-day attacks, the eighth such flaw since the start of the year. "Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said in a Monday security advisory. As Google explained, this flaw stems from a Use-After-Free (UAF) weakness in the XML component of the Google Chrome web browser, which occurs when the browser's XML parser processes data, deletes an object from the computer's memory, but fails to clear the pointer referencing that object. Attackers can exploit this high-severity memory corruption vulnerability when the browser later tries to use or read that "freed" memory space to manipulate the memory layout and execute malicious code. While Google has found evidence of attackers exploiting this zero-day bug in the wild, it has not shared additional details about these incidents. "Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix. We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed," it noted. Google has now fixed the zero-day for users in the Stable Desktop channel, with new versions rolling out to Windows, macOS (157.0.8103.50/.51), and Linux users (157.0.8103.50). Although Google says the security update could take days or weeks to reach all Chrome users, it was available immediately when BleepingComputer checked for updates today. If you don't want to update the web browser manually, you can also let Chrome check for updates on its own, as it will automatically install them after the next launch. ​Since the start of the year, Google has addressed seven other actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities: An iterator invalidation bug (CVE-2026-2441) in CSSFontFeatureValuesMap (Chrome's implementation of CSS font feature values), which Google addressed in mid-February. Two other Chrome zero-day bugs exploited in attacks were patched in March: an out-of-bounds write weakness in the Skia 2D graphics library (CVE-2026-3909), and an inappropriate implementation vulnerability in the V8 JavaScript and WebAssembly engine (CVE-2026-3910). A use-after-free weakness in Dawn (CVE-2026-5281), the underlying cross-platform implementation of the WebGPU standard used by the Chromium project, which Google patched in April. An out-of-bounds read and write vulnerability in Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine (CVE-2026-11645), exploited in the wild and patched in June. And out-of-bounds write (CVE-2026-87491) and type confusion (CVE-2026-85046) flaws in the V8 JavaScript engine, fixed in September. Google fixed eight more zero-days exploited in attacks in 2025, many of them reported by the company's Threat Analysis Group (TAG), which tracks zero-day exploits used in spyware attacks. 1fa3i4t.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Application Security Anthropic on Monday released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models, which it said exhibit improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. During pre-release training, the large language models (LLMs) helped its engineers "complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours." The artificial intelligence (AI) company said high-stakes risks arising from misalignment remain low, and claimed the models matched or performed better than Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most alignment measures, resistance to misuse, honesty, and factuality. "It was roughly an order of magnitude less likely than Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 to publish harmful content to public package registries without encouragement, though it still did so when encouraged by the simulated user," Anthropic noted in its system card. On Irregular's CyScenarioBench, which measures whether a model can plan and execute a multi-stage cyber operation in a realistic environment, Fable 5.2 completed 76.3% of all challenges, compared to 61.7% for Fable 5.1 and 61% for OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber. In a pair of reports published over the last month, Irregular said Google's Gemini 4 Argon solved 12 challenges in the subset of the CyScenarioBench suite end to end, up from 5 for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and none for Gemini 3.1 Pro. "On CyScenarioBench, GPT-6 Cyber completed 11 of 11 long-horizon scenarios at least once, compared with 8 of 11 for GPT-6 Astra. Its average success rate was 61%, an increase of 7 percentage points," the AI testing lab said. "On Atomic Challenges, GPT-6 Cyber solved all 22 challenges. Average success rates were 97% in vulnerability research and exploitation, 98% in network attack simulation, and 63% in evasion." Fable 5.2 also scored 89.6% on the CVE Rediscovery benchmark, Anthropic's own internal evaluation of whether an AI model can independently rediscover known vulnerabilities given only the affected source code. The assessment includes 1,829 advisories for open-source projects published in October 2026. Describing Claude Mythos 5.2 as its "most capable model for cybersecurity engineering," Anthropic said it can flag more vulnerabilities than prior models, while simultaneously getting better at reproducing and fixing them. As before, the model's cyber capabilities are accessible through its Cyber Verification Program. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. The development comes as Anthropic updated Claude Security with continuous code scanning and automatic fix tracking to help security teams monitor and address vulnerabilities as code changes. "Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project's threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what's actually reachable first," Anthropic said.

qvoq93.text: AI infrastructure startup Fireworks has disclosed a new security breach in which attackers accessed its development machines after breaching a third-party cloud provider. FireWorks provides a high-performance inference platform for developers who want to deploy and run open-source artificial intelligence models (such as Mistral, Meta's Llama, or Google's Gemma) without worrying about hardware bottlenecks and complex infrastructure tasks. The company notified law enforcement and customers of another security incident in early October after attackers accessed environment variables containing API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts. "The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to Large Language Models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways, known as 'LLMJacking'," Fireworks said at the time. After revoking compromised internal credentials, affected Fireworks API keys, and keys created by the attackers, Fireworks discovered another security incident on October 23. In the new breach, the threat actors accessed resource metadata (e.g., Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, creation time), billing information (e.g., billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage), and incomplete model weights and datasets for some customers. However, the company said the attackers couldn't access customer payment card numbers because Fireworks doesn't store them. "A third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks R&D machines experienced a security incident on October 23. On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," Fireworks noted in a Monday advisory. "We detected this activity on the same day, and followed our incident response processes to take immediate remediation measures and close known critical vulnerabilities. As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use." Since the attack, Fireworks revoked and replaced credentials and service accounts, restricted unauthorized network pathways, isolated affected systems, and tightened access to data storage and analytics systems to block public or unauthorized access to stored data. The company is now working with Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 incident response division to secure its systems against future attacks and further investigate the incident's full scope and impact. One week ago, researchers at Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant reported that large language model hijacking attacks (also known as LLMjacking) are driving record costs for compromised organizations, with cloud AI charges reaching as high as $1 million due to fraudulent calls using stolen API keys. oj5ea3.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Browser Security Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component. Use-after-free bugs typically occur when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has already been freed. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to achieve data corruption, program crashes, or arbitrary code execution. An anonymous security researcher has been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw on November 6, 2026. Google acknowledged it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," but has not revealed any additional specific information related to how it's being abused in real-world attacks or who is behind them. "Access to bug details and links may be kept restricted until a majority of users are updated with a fix," the tech giant added. "We will also retain restrictions if the bug exists in a third-party library that other projects similarly depend on, but haven't yet fixed." With the latest development, Google has addressed a total of eight actively exploited Chrome zero-days since the start of the year. This includes CVE-2026-2441, CVE-2026-3909, CVE-2026-3910, CVE-2026-5281, CVE-2026-11645, CVE-2026-85046, and CVE-2026-87491. For optimal protection, users are advised to update their Chrome browser to versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Apple macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. To ensure the latest updates are installed, users can navigate to More > Help > About Google Chrome and select Relaunch. Users of other Chromium-based browsers, such as Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, are also advised to apply the fixes as and when they become available.

kqrepa.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security N-able said it has taken N-central Hosted Environments offline and is urging on-premises customers to shut down their servers until further notice following the public disclosure of over 30 vulnerabilities collectively tracked as Able2Shell. "As a precautionary measure, we are temporarily taking our Hosted N-central environment offline while we take the necessary actions to secure the environment and implement appropriate remediation," N-able said. "During this time, customers will be unable to access their Hosted N-central classic environment, and associated services may be unavailable. However, the Ecoverse services under N-able Login remain available and online, including Asset View, Patching, Vulnerability Management, scripting, policies and tagging." The company also said it has not observed any signs of active exploitation of these vulnerabilities, adding it's currently working on a hot fix to address them. The following services are impacted - N-central (hosted version) (Americas) N-central (hosted version) (APAC) N-central (hosted version) (Europe) N-central On-premise (Americas) N-central On-premise (APAC) N-central On-premise (Europe) The development comes as independent security researcher Sean Bales disclosed multiple security flaws along with proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. The researcher said the issues were tested against N-able N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31. The identified zero-day vulnerabilities include credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, cross-site scripting (XSS), XML external entity (XXE) injection, and remote code execution (RCE) flaws - Multiple N-central zero-days enable anonymous credential theft, administrator creation, and nable/root RCE. Chains include XXE/NCI trust abuse, support-token theft, unsigned NSP execution, XSS-to-OGNL, and authenticated reverse shells. Arbitrary file writes, traversal, credential disclosure, MDM impersonation, audit tampering, and privileged-helper injection. A native GenericTCP stack overflow also achieves root command execution Successful exploitation of these flaws can allow rogue administrative access to the N-central management interface and facilitate command execution as root. Update watchTowr, in a post shared on X, said it "observed exploitation attempts against N-able N-central honeypots overnight following the 'Able2Shell' zero-days being dropped." The preemptive exposure management firm is urging users to audit for signs of compromise, restrict access, and follow vendor guidance on mitigation steps.

tiwutz.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday added four security flaws impacting GPUStack, SignalWire FreeSwitch, OpenBSD OpenSSH, and IBM Aspera Faspex to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-123218 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability in IBM Aspera Faspex that could allow an authenticated user to craft a specific message to bypass authorization, causing privilege escalations. (Fixed in November 2026) CVE-2026-116779 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in SignalWire FreeSwitch that could result in configuration and credential disclosure, arbitrary call control, and command execution. (Fixed in October 2026) CVE-2026-123158 aka SSHole (CVSS score: 8.1) - An unexpected status code or return value vulnerability in OpenBSD OpenSSH on Linux that could allow for authentication bypass. (Fixed in November 2026) CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper authentication vulnerability in GPUStack that could allow improper authentication vulnerability which could allow unauthenticated administrative access, including user and model changes, persistent administrator API-key creation, disclosure of worker and cloud-provider secrets, and code execution through POST /v2/inference-backends/from-yaml. (Fixed in July 2026) The addition of CVE-2026-123158 to the KEV catalog follows reports of exploitation attempts targeting the flaw since November 6, 2026. A total of 22 exploitation attempts have been recorded from 14 unique IP addresses so far, according to Previdian. In a post shared on X on November 7, 2026, Defused Cyber said it "observed a small amount of actors targeting SSHole" but stressed the exploitation activity is not widespread yet. According to GreyNoise, the first exploitation attempt against its honeypot network was observed on November 7, 2026, at 12:46 a.m. UTC. Confirmed post-exploitation activity has been detected from six source IP addresses, representing 18 distinct attack chains to date. These involve reconnaissance, queries to cloud metadata services, attempts to read password hashes and root SSH keys, and efforts to modify the SSH authorized_keys file to gain persistent access. In at least one case, an unknown threat actor dubbed GT10 has been observed deploying TAC Agent, a Python-based command-and-control (C2) agent capable of shell command execution, system reconnaissance, directory enumeration, file transfer, and updating itself. Threat intelligence firm watchTowr said it has also observed the OpenSSH flaw being weaponized in the wild for botnet and cryptocurrency miner activity. In an advisory for CVE-2026-102895 published on July 31, 2026, the maintainers of the GPUStack Python package credited Nikko Enggaliano, Wei Yunzhou, Rui Yang, and Haoyu Wang for independently reporting the flaw, adding that "active in-the-wild exploitation" was reported by Ulex Innovative Systems' Javier Sixto. There are currently no public reports on how the other vulnerabilities are being exploited, who is behind them, and the scale of such efforts. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 12, 2026.

1itlbp9.text: Vanderbilt University warns it is responding to a cyberattack claimed by the BYOD ransomware gang, which claims to have encrypted the university's databases and stolen sensitive student, employee, and research data. The university confirmed the incident Monday, warning that university devices, systems, and cloud-based services may be affected. "We are currently responding to an active cybersecurity incident that may impact university devices, systems, and cloud-based services. Our Information Technology team is actively investigating and working to contain the situation," Vanderbilt said in a statement on X. As part of its response, the university told students, faculty, and staff to shut down university devices, disconnect from university Wi-Fi, and watch for suspicious activity. The university warned that signs of compromise may include unexpected pop-ups or security notifications, unusual changes to files or permissions in cloud storage platforms, missing or modified files, unfamiliar applications, and unexpected authentication requests. Those who notice suspicious activity were instructed not to investigate or troubleshoot the issue themselves, but instead immediately shut down their devices and contact the university's IT service desk. Vanderbilt has not publicly disclosed the nature of the attack or confirmed whether any data was stolen. BleepingComputer contacted Vanderbilt University with questions about the attack, including whether systems were encrypted, what data may have been stolen, and whether the incident has been contained. If you have any information regarding this incident or other undisclosed attacks, you can contact us confidentially via Signal at 646-961-3731 or at tips@bleepingcomputer.com. BYOD ransomware claims attack On Monday, the BYOD ransomware group claimed responsibility for the attack on its data leak site, alleging that it had encrypted Vanderbilt's databases and stolen sensitive information belonging to students and employees. "If you could not tell already, your databases are locked, We have your entire estate and research data. Over 1 Million SSNs, Full Names, Email addresses, Phone Numbers, Student & Employee Records, Full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess," reads the BYOD data leak site. BYOD ransomware group claims attack on Vanderbilt University Source: BleepingComputer BleepingComputer has since received a photograph of an alleged computer screen showing icons associated with Vanderbilt University and displaying a BYOD ransom note named "README_BYOD_31.txt". The ransom note includes a link to the BYOD data leak site and contact information for the SESSION encrypted messaging platform to negotiate with the ransomware gang. BleepingComputer can confirm that the link in the ransom note is the site operated by BYOD. "Oh no, you have been compromised by BYOD :<," reads the ransom note. "We have all of your data including your backups, your entire network is compromised." "Yes, this affects your student and employee data the most, every single SSN is archived, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, work addresses, roles, birthdays, quite literally everything." Photograph of BYOD ransom note displayed on a Vanderbilt University computer Source: BleepingComputer The note also threatens to release stolen data and cause further disruption if the university does not negotiate with the attackers. A video shared on YouTube and with BleepingComputer also shows how infected devices are playing audio warning that the network has been compromised by "BYOD". While the ransom note and video indicate BYOD is behind the attack, Vanderbilt has not officially confirmed the group's involvement or whether devices were encrypted. BYOD is a relatively new ransomware gang that launched in 2026 and currently lists 5 other organizations on its data leak site. Last month, the ransomware gang claimed responsibility for an attack on the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center in a cyberattack that caused system outages and disrupted patient care and academic activities. nsr45r.text: Japanese gaming giant SEGA has disclosed that a data breach at its third-party newsletter provider, ARARA, exposed the email addresses of 2.2 million newsletter subscribers. The company says the exposed data also includes 92,300 records with additional information yet to be determined. The breach affects 11 newsletters linked to SEGA and SEGA Fave products and services. The investigation found that the compromised data did not include customer names, dates of birth, gender, addresses, phone numbers, credit card details, or account passwords. Also, email addresses registered with a “SEGA Account” are handled by a separate distribution system and were not affected by this incident. The company is working with ARARA to determine what data was exposed and says it has no confirmed evidence of misuse. “We are currently investigating the information associated with newsletter distribution in cooperation with ARARA,” SEGA stated. ARARA service breached ARARA disclosed on November 2 that it suffered a massive breach affecting its email distribution service, which compromised 77 million email addresses from nearly 380 corporate clients. According to the company, a web server vulnerability and problems in its system environment contributed to the incident, but the exact intrusion method and timing remain under investigation. ARARA previously estimated a smaller impact and assured SEGA on October 29 that no data compromise had occurred. However, on November 3, after uncovering the full extent of the incident, ARARA notified the gaming company that data had been exposed and shared the full details between November 5 and 8. ARARA also said the attackers abused their access to its service to send over 7 million emails impersonating credit card companies in late October. Other notable victims of the same incident include MOS Burger, with 7.5 million email addresses exposed, Shochiku Multiplex Theatres, with 3.3 million records, TKC, with 2.3 million email addresses, and IIJmio, with nearly 1 million email addresses. SEGA Arcade still down SEGA Fave’s arcade game network services, which suffered a separate cybersecurity incident last week, are still offline, undergoing maintenance and safety checks. On November 2, SEGA FAVE, SEGA's subsidiary responsible for toys, electronic gadgets, and arcade machine operations, disclosed unauthorized access to servers supporting its ALL.Net and Aime arcade gaming network services. In response, it suspended all related services, including online gameplay, SEGA Lucky Kuji Online, and new SEGA ID registrations. Its initial investigation found no evidence of customer or business partner data exfiltration, while payment information was unaffected because it was stored separately. SEGA noted that the two incidents are unrelated. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. 283ui0.text: N-able has taken its hosted N-central environments offline and urged on-premises customers to shut down their servers after a security researcher publicly disclosed more than 30 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities, including exploits that could let attackers take over vulnerable systems. Security researcher Sean Bales disclosed the vulnerabilities late Sunday, November 8, and published a GitHub repository called Able2Shell containing proof-of-concept exploits for the flaws. N-central is a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform used by managed service providers (MSPs) and IT teams to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The researcher says the vulnerabilities were tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release version of the software, and believes most, if not all, flaws also affect earlier versions. Bales also confirmed to BleepingComputer that the discovery of the vulnerabilities was AI-assisted. The disclosed vulnerabilities include authentication bypasses, credential disclosure, arbitrary file writes, directory traversal, cross-site scripting (XSS), XML external entity (XXE) injection, and remote code execution (RCE) flaws. One of the most critical exploit chains abuses an unauthenticated XXE vulnerability in N-central's service-import functionality to steal a trusted local session, reset an account password, and execute commands on the server as the nable user. The same exploit can also create an enabled Default Administrator account with attacker-controlled credentials, providing rogue administrative access to the N-central management interface. Bales shared a video demonstration of this exploit, showing terminal output reporting successful administrator account creation, login authentication, access to protected administrative functionality, and remote command execution as the nable user. Other disclosed exploits include a stored XSS that can execute commands as root when an administrator views malicious patch metadata, and a privilege-escalation flaw that allows code running under the nable account to execute commands as root. Bales confirmed to BleepingComputer that the unauthenticated XXE-to-RCE exploit was the most critical of the disclosed vulnerabilities. N-able takes servers offline worldwide After the disclosure, N-able announced a critical security incident and took its hosted N-central environments offline across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific regions. While BleepingComputer has not independently verified all the reported vulnerabilities, N-able confirmed it is developing a hotfix to address the security issues, lending credence to the researcher's claims that at least some of the flaws are legitimate zero-days. "N-able is actively responding to non-responsible communication of critical vulnerabilities in N-central late Sunday night, November 8, found by an independent researcher," N-able told BleepingComputer. "As a precautionary measure, we took our Hosted N-central environment offline today, November 9, and provided guidance to customers operating on-premises N-central servers to temporarily take their servers offline until further notice." "Our Security, Engineering, and Operations teams are actively working to implement the necessary remediation. At this time, we have not observed active exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Protecting our customers and their environments remains our highest priority, and we will provide additional updates as they become available." In a subsequent status update, N-able said it was continuing to develop and validate a hotfix and had found no evidence of active exploitation or unauthorized data access. While the N-central classic environment is unavailable, N-able said Ecoverse services accessed through N-able Login remain operational. N-able has not provided an estimate of when N-central will come back online but says it plans to publish updates every four hours, or sooner if new information becomes available. Researcher claims previous vulnerability reports ignored Bales told BleepingComputer that he deliberately released the N-central vulnerabilities without notifying N-able beforehand because the company allegedly failed to address vulnerabilities he had previously reported in a different N-able product. According to Bales, he disclosed two unrelated remote code execution vulnerabilities and a privilege-escalation flaw approximately five to six months ago, but those vulnerabilities remain unpatched. "I disclosed 2 unrelated RCEs for a different N-able product, along with a priv esc vulnerability 5 or 6 months ago. These have yet to be patched. I did not disclose any of the 0-days I posted last night," Bales told BleepingComputer. He also claims to have sent follow-up emails over the past four to six weeks without a response. Bales says his previous experience with N-able's vulnerability disclosure process and that "they don't take disclosure seriously" led him to publish the N-central zero-day exploits. However, he said these exploits target a different N-able product than the ones he previously disclosed. The researcher also claimed that he received no payment through N-able's bug bounty platform for his earlier reports. Bales confirmed that N-able executives, including the company's CEO and CTO, contacted him following the disclosure and asked him to remove the GitHub repository and work with the company. "They did not threaten me or anything though. Only asked to take down the repo, work with them, etc." BleepingComputer asked N-able about Bales' allegations concerning the previously disclosed vulnerabilities, their patching status, and the alleged lack of responses to his follow-up emails. However, the company did not address those questions, providing only the statement concerning the N-central security incident and the precautionary shutdown. The previously reported vulnerabilities are not included in the publicly released Able2Shell repository and allegedly remain unpatched. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. euksqu.text: International healthcare company Amplifon said thousands of its U.S. customers had their Social Security numbers and medical information stolen during a cyberattack in February. The Milan, Italy, company pairs patients in need of hearing aids and auditory assistance with device providers and services. Amplifon began notifying state regulators of a data breach last week, telling Texas officials that 85,804 people were impacted by the security incident in addition to 1,027 people in Vermont. The company also filed breach notices in California. In a breach notice on its U.S. website, Amplifon said it initially discovered suspicious activity on February 11, with an investigation later revealing the hackers had access to company files between January 18 and February 8. The stolen data includes names, driver’s licenses, state IDs, medical information, health insurance data and financial information. No hacking group has taken credit for the incident as of Monday. Several class action law firms said the total number of victims is 1,332,826, but Amplifon did not respond to requests for confirmation. Amplifon was founded in 1950 for World War II veterans suffering from hearing loss and expanded to the U.S., Asia and Africa — now covering more than 28 countries across five continents. The company works with patients to find the right hearing devices and offer tests as well as other hearing-related healthcare services. The healthcare industry, particularly companies producing wearable devices, has faced an unprecedented level of attack in 2026 by cybercriminals. Medical device maker iRhythm said last month that 8,179,772 people were impacted by a cyberattack on their systems. Medical device makers like Medtronic, Boston Scientific, Stryker, UFP, Masimo, Surmodics, Artivion and Zoll have dealt with cybersecurity incidents that exposed the sensitive medical data of millions and caused supply chain issues. No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

1cmpi0g.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 09, 2026Cloud Security / Data Breach An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today. The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed. Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions. The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole, must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID. Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked. Any organization that has connected Qubole to AWS, even one that no longer uses it, should check its CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward. The sign to look for is an AssumeRole request from the account Qubole's platform uses, 805246085872, that came from an address outside AWS. The researchers did not say whether the credentials have since been disabled or whether the activity has stopped. Neither Qubole nor Idera had posted a statement about the attack on their websites when The Hacker News checked today. Why the Roles Let the Attacker In Every AssumeRole request tied to the attacker carried an External ID and was accepted, the researchers said in their technical analysis. AWS accepts an AssumeRole request for such a role when it comes from the trusted account and includes the correct External ID. The code is not treated as a secret, and anyone with access to the role can view it, according to AWS's external ID guidance. Sentra spotted the activity in several of its customers' environments and alerted the researchers. In the accounts the researchers examined, the attacker looked for stored credentials. It read environment variables for Lambda functions, pulled secrets from Secrets Manager, and read values from the SSM Parameter Store. It then ran the credentials it had found through TruffleHog to test whether they worked. These were the victims' own AWS access keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials. The attacker also copied data out of S3. It retrieved data from any bucket a role could access rather than searching for specific data, and sometimes downloaded an entire bucket in a single session. The researchers have not linked this campaign to any other publicly reported activity, and say the targeting does not match what state-backed groups usually go after. Qubole also lets customers connect with AWS access keys instead of a role. From October 8 to October 11, an attacker used customers' own AWS access keys, which the researchers believe had been set up for Qubole. That attacker then compromised a few of the victims' cloud environments. This activity has not been linked to the AssumeRole abuse. How to Check Your Accounts Wiz's hunting guidance covers CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward in every AWS account that holds a Qubole role. Look for: Account: AssumeRole requests where userIdentity.accountId is 805246085872 and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. The researchers saw Qubole's real traffic come only from AWS. IAM principal ID: AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined. IAM principal ID: AIDAJYRRH5Y3A7AAJM2HW, when the source address is outside AWS. The attacker used this IAM user from October 18, but Qubole's normal traffic also uses it. IP: 57.129.54[.]120 and 2001:41d0:70d[:]7800::, OVH-hosted addresses that the attacker used. IP: 45.83.220[.]211, 185.209.199[.]73 and 89.37.63[.]175, which are Mullvad VPN addresses. Other VPN users share them, so a match alone is not proof. Session name: role sessions that start with quiam-, such as quiam-enum. User agent: TruffleHog on GetCallerIdentity calls from one of the IP addresses above. Look for the same user agent in your identity provider's sign-in logs. For every suspicious session, review everything it did afterward, especially in Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda, and S3. CloudTrail management events log each AssumeRole request and bucket listing, but not which S3 objects were read. That needs S3 data events or S3 server access logs. Several victims lacked the required logs, so responders could not determine which objects the attacker had read. How to Close the Route The researchers recommend these steps: If the attacker assumed one of your Qubole roles, rotate all secrets, parameters, and Lambda environment variables that role had access to, and revoke the role's active sessions. Rotating a credential does not end sessions that were already issued. Remove any Qubole role you no longer need, or take Qubole's account out of its trust policy. Where Qubole supports it, swap the account-wide :root principal in the trust policy for the specific IAM principal that Qubole uses. Add an aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce condition that limits AssumeRole requests to the vendor's documented network ranges. In this attack, the researchers said, "a source IP condition alone would have blocked every role assumption we observed." Assume others can see the External ID. It is logged in plain text in CloudTrail, and vendors and infrastructure-as-code files often store it, so do not use it as your only control. After an incident like this, change it to Qubole and use a different value for each role where possible. Review what each vendor role can reach. Qubole's setup guide includes a sample S3 policy that lets the role read every bucket in the account. Vendor roles are often granted access to Lambda settings, Secrets Manager, SSM parameters, and broad S3 read permissions for convenience, according to the researchers. Set alerts for AssumeRole requests from a vendor account that arrive through a VPN or a hosting company the vendor has not used before. Log every account and region with an organization trail, and enable S3 data events or server access logs for buckets that store sensitive data.

15lo983.text: Attackers used the Ethersphere project's own release automation to publish malicious versions of two of its tools for the Swarm decentralized storage network: bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2. Both releases download and run code built to steal the wallet key that Swarm Desktop keeps for its node, along with the stored password that unlocks it. The code is also built to install a backdoor on Windows, macOS, and Linux machines. The bee-js package is the JavaScript library behind Swarm Desktop and the swarm-cli command-line tool. Swarm Desktop runs a Swarm node on a user's own computer and saves the node's private keys there. Both malicious releases have been taken down, and the project's maintainers released a clean Swarm Desktop update today. Neither step removes a backdoor already installed nor protects a key already sent. No theft of funds had been reported at the time of writing. Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 appeared on GitHub at about 00:36 UTC today and was withdrawn about 8.5 hours later. The app's built-in updater could offer it to Windows x64 computers and Apple Silicon Macs within about 10 minutes, according to an incident analysis by Socket, a supply chain security firm. Intel Macs were never offered it, and Linux installs do not update automatically. The bee-js release, version 13.3.0, was the latest version on npm for about 75 minutes, from 00:09 to 01:25 UTC today. Its code runs as a postinstall script, which npm executes automatically during installation unless install scripts are disabled. A project did not need to import the library for the code to run. The project's own swarm-cli and bee-dashboard packages, and the Swarm Desktop source code, accepted version ranges that included 13.3.0. A fresh install within that window could have pulled in the malicious version. None of the reports gave a count of infected machines. The firm's rough estimate is that bee-js 13.3.0 was downloaded about 10 times, including by security scanners and mirrors. Swarm Desktop 0.56.2's download count reached 65 by 08:27 UTC, including researchers. Ethersphere's maintainers withdrew 0.56.2 and replaced it today with a clean release, version 0.56.3. In the change that set up the new release, one of them wrote that 0.56.2 "was published by an attacker using stolen CI credentials and has been withdrawn." Version 0.56.3 is the same code as the previous version, 0.56.1, signed with a newly issued Developer ID certificate, according to that maintainer's incident note. The note says the app's auto-updater will move installs of 0.56.2 to it, although Linux packages still need to be replaced by hand. A comparison of the two versions' source code by The Hacker News found no changes beyond the version number and release notes. When The Hacker News checked npm today, 13.2.0 was again the latest bee-js version, and 13.3.0 could no longer be downloaded from the registry. What to Do The GitHub advisory for bee-js 13.3.0 says: "Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised." SafeDep, a software supply chain security company, offers the same advice for any computer on which Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 was installed. If you use bee-js in a project or CI job: Search lockfiles, package caches, internal registries, and CI install logs for @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0, including copies pulled in by other packages. Pin 13.2.0, and clear cached copies of 13.3.0, including any npm mirror you install through. If 13.3.0 was installed with install scripts turned on, treat that machine or CI runner as compromised, even if the install log shows no errors. The code hides its own network errors. From a clean computer, rotate every password, token, and key that the installing user or CI job could read. If you run Swarm Desktop: Look for the line Bee Desktop version: 0.56.2 (production) in the app's log file, bee-desktop.log. Version 0.56.2 is written at every launch, just before the malicious code runs. The log folder is ~/Library/Logs/Swarm Desktop/ on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Swarm Desktop\Log\ on Windows, and ~/.local/state/Swarm Desktop/ on Linux. Install 0.56.3. On Linux, replace the package by hand. If 0.56.2 ever ran, treat the node's key and password as stolen. From a clean computer, move the node's funds, chequebook, and stake to a new key. On any machine where the code ran: Remove the ~/.solidity/ folder, the solidity-langsupport-runner.service user service on Linux, the com.solidity.langsupport.runner LaunchAgent on macOS, and the ScreenConnect Client (5cbe79c9c25524df) service on Windows. Updating, reinstalling, or removing the app or package does not remove them. Where possible, rebuild the machine from a trusted image instead of cleaning it in place. How the Malware Works Both releases carry the same loader, SafeDep found in its technical analysis. It is a few lines of code that download more code from api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz and run it with the user's permissions. In bee-js the loader is the postinstall script, and in Swarm Desktop it runs each time the app starts. The downloaded code looks for two files in Swarm Desktop's data folder: config.yaml and data-dir/keys/swarm.key. If both are there, it sends them to the attackers' server. The key file is an encrypted Ethereum keystore, but Swarm Desktop keeps its password in plain text in config.yaml. With both files, the attackers can take the node wallet's xDAI and xBZZ tokens, its chequebook funds, and its stake, the company says. The downloaded code also installs a backdoor. On Linux and macOS, it is a Go remote shell called evjawbreaker, saved in a hidden ~/.solidity folder. It runs in the background as a user service on Linux and as a LaunchAgent on macOS. The shell reads the address of its control server from an Ethereum smart contract, so the attackers can change that address at any time. They had updated it 29 minutes before the malicious bee-js code was added. On Windows, the downloaded code installs a genuine ScreenConnect remote-access client, signed by its maker, ConnectWise. The client runs as a system service and connects to the attackers' relay. If the user is an administrator, the code gets administrator rights through a known way around the User Account Control prompt. If not, it shows the prompt again whenever the user cancels. With those rights, it adds a Microsoft Defender exclusion and installs the client silently. How the Releases Got Out Both releases came from bee-worker, the account Ethersphere uses to automate its releases. Neither change was signed nor submitted as a pull request. For bee-js, the attackers published a GitHub release for the new version, which started the project's npm publishing workflow. That workflow needed no approval and published the package to npm in 73 seconds, according to Socket. Because the project's real workflow built it, the package carried valid provenance, the record that links an npm package to the repository and workflow that built it. Provenance shows where a package was built, not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it. For Swarm Desktop, the attackers manually started a build workflow that had the project's Apple and Windows signing certificates and needed no approval. The macOS app was signed with the project's Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so macOS displayed only its normal first-launch prompt, the firm found. The maintainers have since made the app's signing jobs wait for approval from the project's DevOps team and run only from the main branch. How the attackers gained access remained unclear at the time of writing. The maintainer's incident note blames the theft of CI credentials and secrets. The firm's analysis indicates that two GitHub accounts were used: bee-worker and a long-time maintainer's account. None of the reports explained how the credentials were stolen. Links to Earlier Attacks The payloads share an Ethereum contract, a ScreenConnect relay, and file names with fake extensions for Solidity developers that appeared on the Open VSX marketplace in September. Researchers at Pluto Security described those extensions in their October 1 EtherDuck analysis. Pluto ties them "with high confidence" to the group behind the original SleepyDuck extension, which read its server address from a different Ethereum contract in 2025. Socket says the same group is behind the bee-js and Swarm Desktop releases. Indicators of Compromise Defenders can search logs and machines for the following.
