ffgpri.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday. The attacker could also have seen requests being processed on that server that day, including requests sent in confidential mode, the company said earlier this week. That mode processes requests inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) designed to keep them private even from the company itself. But the TEE "does not protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside the environment," the company said. SGLang runs inside the TEE, which is how the attacker could reach requests there. That access has since been closed, but not before the attacker moved further into the company's systems. The attacker reached an internal system behind Private Chat, a product the company had already deprecated. So far, the company has confirmed that the attacker downloaded account details for about 100 users there. These are email addresses and names, and for some accounts, plan and balance information. The company found no sign that stored Private Chat conversations or uploaded files were accessed. The attacker also reached 18 AI agents on an older deployment of NEAR AI Agents that did not run inside the company's TEE. From those agents, the attacker took data including chat history, settings and logs. Two customers' NEAR AI Cloud API keys were exposed in logs. The company has revoked both. After detecting the attack, the company revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens and took Private Chat offline. It also deployed a fix for the SGLang flaw on all of its inference servers, rotated its remaining credentials and completed a full forensic review, according to its incident report. Access to its NEAR AI Cloud service has been restored. The company reported the flaw to the SGLang project. It has not identified the flaw by CVE number, named the affected SGLang versions, or said whether the project has released a fix. The company has contacted users whose account details or agents it confirmed were accessed. Affected users heard directly from security@near.ai, with the steps that apply to them. As a precaution, the company asks users to be careful with messages about their account or balance that they did not ask for. In a follow-up post yesterday, it said users who have not heard from it do not need to do anything. It has not said whether people whose requests passed through the affected server last Sunday were among those contacted. In an October 15 technical write-up, Brave, the browser maker, said its Leo assistant runs chats with the GLM 5.3 Flash model inside a TEE operated by NEAR AI. NEAR AI has not said whether the affected server handled any of those chats.

1n1nuo.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack French software company Vates VMS has warned of a critical security vulnerability in Xen Orchestra that it said is being actively exploited in the wild. The authentication bypass flaw, which does not yet have a CVE identifier, is tracked as VSA-2026-062. "REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}," Vates VMS said in an alert. "REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string." "The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs." In other words, the vulnerability can allow an attacker to bypass authentication by sending a specially crafted cookie and perform arbitrary actions with "Admin" privileges, ultimately resulting in arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root. Vates VMS said it's seeing the vulnerability being actively exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain - 91.211.251[.]112:8001, which has been flagged as a RedLine Stealer command-and-control (C2) server on VirusTotal ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333 It's unclear when the activity started and if the vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day. Other indicators of compromise are listed below - HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{} A running virtual machine named pivot2 Virtual machines configured using "hvm_serial: file" parameter Suspicious files named /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6 The issue has been addressed in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 for the stable and latest channels, as well as xo-server versions 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. If immediate patching is not an option, the following mitigations are advised - Avoid exposing Xen Orchestra instances on the internet Block the IP address and domain associated with malicious activity Block the empty token in a web application firewall (WAF) or a reverse proxy Rotate all passwords and secrets in Vates VMS if indicators of compromise are detected Filip Magic (@mad31k) and Christoffer Olsen from TDC NET Security have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw.

1czc3sl.text: Three distinct threat activity clusters with shared infrastructure and malware code similarities have been observed targeting telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions, and critical infrastructure across Latin America, Asia, and Europe over the past year. Check Point Research is tracking the clusters under the names SilentDelivery, OceanGate, and DarkWire. Although initially assumed to be independent sets of attacks, each with its own backdoors and post-exploitation tooling, they have all been linked through a malware ecosystem called Sparrow. The entity behind the Sparrow framework has been codenamed CopperDragon, and is assessed to be a digital quartermaster developing tools for China-nexus threat actors, including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, Tropic Trooper, UAT-9244, and UAT-8302. "Each cluster employed a different toolset and different initial access techniques, including compromising internet-facing infrastructure and highly selective watering hole attacks," Check Point said in a technical report published today. "The compromised websites that were used for watering hole attacks were of government, shipping, and IT and research sectors." Attacks mounted by FamousSparrow are known for deploying backdoors like SparrowDoor (and its variants Crowdoor and TernDoor), SparroWocky, and HemiGate. It's also assessed to share some degree of overlap with Salt Typhoon. However, the precise nature of the relationship remains unclear. The cyber espionage ecosystem linked to CopperDragon is driven by three prominent clusters - SilentDelivery (Beginning in early 2026), which conducts highly selective watering hole attacks targeting Europe and Asia that distribute a backdoor called SquadC (aka SquawkDoor) through trojanized MSI installers masquerading as certificate repair utilities OceanGate (2025-2026), which primarily focuses on Asian organizations with a variant of SparrowDoor after obtaining initial access via internet-facing Linux servers and then moving laterally into Windows environments DarkWire (Mid 2025), which targets telecommunications providers and government organizations across Latin America using backdoors called CopperDoor (aka SparroWocky) and CopperDNS SilentDelivery The SilentDelivery chain begins with the attacker injecting heavily obfuscated JavaScript into legitimate websites frequented by their intended targets. Visitors to the sites are greeted by a Google Chrome SSL certificate warning that instructs users to install a "Certificate Fix" utility to restore access. The so-called utility, once deployed, delivers either SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant. All the compromised websites have been found to be related to government, shipping, IT, and research sectors in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong, and Indonesia. According to a report published by Positive Technologies in August 2026, there are indications that the campaign has also targeted entities in Egypt and the Philippines using this method. "The JavaScript injected into the compromised websites is heavily obfuscated using jsjiami, a publicly available JavaScript obfuscation service," Check Point said. "It first checks whether the user is running Windows and, in some cases, verifies that the website’s domain matches the intended compromised domain." The script then repeatedly sends status-check requests to a command-and-control (C2) server to fingerprint the user based on IP and geolocation, and ultimately decide whether to continue the attack and serve the fake warning. Source: Positive Technologies Written in C/C++, SquadC is a Windows backdoor that enables initial foothold over the infected host. It establishes persistence by means of a Windows Registry Run key that masquerades as a Windows update assistant. Further analysis has uncovered that the malware is also distributed via phishing emails targeting Indonesian organizations. The phishing email comes with a Windows Shortcut (LNK) disguised as a PDF document, which, when opened, abuses the legitimate "ftp.exe" binary to run a batch script that's responsible for displaying an empty file as a decoy, while launching SquadC via DLL sideloading. OceanGate The OceanGate operation, on the other hand, has been observed targeting both Windows and Linux environments, deploying previously undocumented tooling to maintain access, move laterally across the network, and exfiltrate sensitive data. The Linux phase of the attack involves two new backdoors - AnnobinDoor, a Go-based backdoor that supports a wide array of features, such as remote access, interactive shell, file management, SOCKS proxying, SSH tunneling, port forwarding, and reverse connections, and enables the infected Linux machine to function as both a remote shell and an internal network pivot SparrowShell, a modular Linux backdoor that shares overlaps with its Windows counterpart, SparrowDoor "After harvesting credentials from multiple users and establishing a strong foothold in the Linux environment, the actor moved into the Windows environment," Check Point explained. "The actor attempted to log in to several Windows machines over RDP, trying different passwords until it successfully authenticated with an administrator account." This step is followed by the deployment of bespoke post-exploitation tools and a variant of SparrowDoor - CopperAdu, a post-exploitation tool which configures a compromised Windows machine for remote administrative access CopperList, a Windows reconnaissance tool for collecting host information, disk details, and a recursive file inventory, including file paths, sizes, and timestamps CopperLogger, a Raw Input-based keylogger to capture keyboard input events, along with monitoring clipboard activity, active window titles, and associated process names and paths CopperLsa, a utility that collects passwords, hashes, and authentication tokens from NTLM and Kerberos What's more, the threat actor has been found incorporating kernel rootkits and kernel-level access capabilities into SparrowDoor and SparrowShell to evade defenses through process hiding and to capture and manipulate network packet capture using WinDivert drivers. "The actor abused the driver to convert SparrowDoor into a passive backdoor that intercepts and manipulates packets at the kernel level, making its traffic less visible," Check Point said. "This allows the backdoor to listen internally on one port while receiving connections through an externally accessible port, such as 443, that is already used by a legitimate service." "The backdoor applies a strict filter to intercept connections from a specific source IP address to the legitimate service's port. It manipulates the packet and rewrites the destination port to the backdoor’s internal listening port, typically a high port such as 49628. For response traffic, it rewrites the source port back to the external service port, making the responses appear to originate from the legitimate service." Interestingly, SparrowShell shares code- and infrastructure-level similarities with a malware called Mélofée that was first described by ExaTrack in March 2023 as based on the open-source Reptile rootkit. This has raised the possibility that CopperDragon is also behind the development and supply of Mélofée. DarkWire The third and last cluster of activity centers around Latin America, with a particular focus on telecommunications operators and government entities. These attacks led to the deployment of two newly identified backdoors called CopperDoor and CopperDNS as a possible replacement for SparrowDoor. Also supporting these operations is a set of custom tools - CopperLoader, a reflective loader typically deployed through DLL sideloading and is used to deliver additional tools, including CopperDoor, CopperDNS, CopperProxy, and CopperLsass CopperDoor, a memory-resident modular backdoor CopperDNS, a CopperDoor variant that communicates through DNS tunneling using MX queries CopperProxy, a SOCKS5 proxy PyProxy, a lightweight UDP relay written in Python CopperLsass, a dedicated module for dumping the LSASS process for credential harvesting "The operation heavily relies on DLL sideloading as a primary execution technique, often abusing executables that are not widely observed among other threat actors in the wild," Check Point said. "To minimize their footprint, the operators deliberately avoided creating new directories on disk, instead placing their tools within existing system paths." "CopperDoor infrastructure demonstrated a higher level of operational security. Most IP addresses were located in Latin America, often within the same country as the victim organization. This proximity likely helps the malicious traffic blend in with legitimate network activity and reduces the chances of detection."

1p3ki8e.text: HomeNewsMicrosoftWindows 11 KB5132061 & KB5131087 cumulative updates released November 10, 2026 01:33 PM Microsoft has released the Patch Tuesday Windows 11 KB513261 and KB5131087 cumulative updates for versions 26H2/25H2/24H2 and 23H2 to fix security vulnerabilities and bugs and add new features. Today's updates are mandatory as they contain the November 2026 Patch Tuesday security patches for hundreds of vulnerabilities discovered in previous months. You can install today's update by going to Start > Settings > Windows Update and clicking on 'Check for Updates.' You can also manually download and install the update from the Microsoft Update Catalog. This is the eleventh 'Patch Tuesday' release in 2026, and it's based on 24H2, which means 25H2 or 26H2 get the same update. There are no exclusive or special changes. You'll get the same fixes across the two versions of Windows 11. What's new in the November 2026 Patch Tuesday update With today's update, Microsoft is adding new customization options to Windows 11 and fixing minor issues with File Explorer. Here's the full list of improvements and fixes: [Context menu in File Explorer] New! This update introduces an updated context menu that is faster, simpler, and more customizable. The updated menu opens more quickly, reduces clutter, and gives you more control over the commands and app extensions that appear when you right-click. You can now customize the context menu to better fit how you use Windows. Select Customize menu at the bottom of the context menu to open its Settings page. Turn built-in Windows commands, such as Send to and Create shortcut, on or off. Add commands such as Print to the context menu. Choose which app extensions appear in the main menu or a submenu or hide the app extensions submenu. Display Cut, Copy, Paste, Rename, Delete, and Share directly in the menu instead of as a row of icons. Move Properties to the bottom of the context menu. To personalize the context menu, right-click and select Customize menu, then choose the commands, app extensions, and layout you prefer. No action is required to use the default configuration. To see more options, hold down Shift and right-click on your desktop. [Modernized AutoPlay experience] New! This update modernizes the AutoPlay dialog that appears when you connect devices such as a phone, camera, or removable drive to your PC. The updated experience supports dark mode, responds better to text scaling and display settings, and makes AutoPlay notifications available in notification center for easier access. [File Explorer] New! Key file information, such as name, location, and date, now appear in a consistent layout on the File Explorer search results page, making search results easier to scan. New! Address bar now supports ~, making it quicker to navigate directly to your user profile folder and subfolders (for example, ~\AppData). New! This update enables dark mode support in the Folder Options dialog in File Explorer. [XBOX mode] New! This update introduces a refreshed Gaming Task View experience in XBOX mode, featuring a new navigation bar that provides quick access to Exit to Desktop and Power Options, making key system actions easier to access while gaming. 1 [Settings] New! This update improves the Privacy & security page in Windows Settings by grouping related Camera, Microphone, and Location privacy controls and elevating usage information from linked pages onto the main page. New! The Device Info card on the Settings Home page, first introduced in the March 2026 preview update KB5079391, is expanding to additional markets. Available to users signed in with a Microsoft account, the card provides a quick view of key PC specifications and usage, with more detailed device information available under Settings > System > About. 1 This update makes some small visual refinements to the design of the temporary files section under Settings > System > Storage. [Phone Link] New! You can now hover over a recent message or notification in the Recent section to preview its content directly in Start without opening the item. This experience can be managed under Phone Link > Settings > Start menu personalization. [Taskbar] New! The update improves animations of app window previews when mousing across app icons in the taskbar. This update improves the underlying state persistence of taskbar settings related to multiple monitors across monitor connections and disconnections. [Magnifier] New! Magnifier now includes a contrast theme toggle that can reduce screen glare while keeping the original colors in photos, videos, and charts. The toggle applies a dark contrast theme by default and is available from the Magnifier toolbar. To choose a different contrast theme, go to Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. Color inversion remains available as a separate option. New! Magnifier now supports per-monitor zoom, allowing each display to use its own zoom level while keeping the magnified view within that display. To use per-monitor zoom, set your displays to Extend under Settings > System > Display. To adjust a display, move your pointer to it and press Windows key + Plus (+) or Windows key + Minus (-), use Ctrl + Alt with the mouse wheel or move the Magnifier toolbar to that display and use its controls. Per-monitor zoom is on by default. You can turn it off or adjust individual zoom levels from the Magnifier toolbar or under Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. New! Magnifier now supports viewport locking for multi-monitor setups with per-monitor zoom turned on. It keeps the magnified view on a display in place while you move the pointer to another display. The locked display remains interactive. Point to a display and press Ctrl + Windows key + K to lock or unlock its view. Press Windows key + Esc to release all locked displays. You can change the lock shortcut to Ctrl + Alt + P under Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. [Live Captions] New! This update improves Live Captions with a new Include screen reader audio setting, which is off by default. With the setting off, Live Captions will not transcribe audio from screen readers such as Narrator, JAWS, and NVDA, keeping captions focused on microphone and system audio. To turn on this setting, go to Settings > Accessibility > Captions. [Narrator] New! Narrator now supports reading and navigating math equations in supported Microsoft 365 apps, including Word and PowerPoint, and supported web content in Microsoft Edge (version 153.0.4234.32 and later) and Google Chrome (version 153.0.8010.18 and later). This makes it easier for users who are blind or have low vision to understand and explore equations, formulas, and scientific notation. Press Narrator key + Alt + N to turn on math navigation and use the arrow keys to explore parts of an equation. Press Esc to exit. Math reading supports English (United States), English (United Kingdom), Traditional Chinese, Finnish, German, and Spanish. You can change the language and other math reading preferences in Narrator settings (Accessibility > Narrator > Math reading). [Family Safety] New! The update improves family safety messaging when applications are blocked because of age-restricted parental controls. [Recovery] New! This update enables Windows recovery (WinRE) to automatically reuse eligible Wi-Fi profiles already saved in Windows, including supported certificate-based networks. Devices can now get online automatically during recovery scenarios such as quick machine recovery or cloud rebuild, without preconfiguring Wi-Fi credentials in WinRE. This capability is on by default, and IT admins can disable it. This feature was previously disclosed last month and is now beginning to roll out. To learn more, see Networking in WinRE. [Cloud rebuild] New! This update introduces Cloud rebuild, a new recovery option that reinstalls Windows 11 using a Windows image and device drivers downloaded from Windows Update, including when Windows is unable to start. No USB media or custom image is required. Cloud rebuild includes: Drive sanitization: Choose to remove your files or securely erase data using the storage hardware’s erase capability before Windows is reinstalled. Sanitization is irreversible. Remote management: IT administrators can configure and start a Cloud rebuild remotely through the Recovery CSP using either the currently installed build or a specified target build. To start Cloud rebuild: In Windows, go to Settings > System > Recovery, and then select Rebuild PC. The device restarts into the Windows Recovery Environment and starts Cloud rebuild. Alternatively, if Windows can't start, the device enters the Windows Recovery Environment automatically after repeated boot failures. From the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE), select Troubleshoot > Recovery and uninstall > Cloud rebuild. Connect to a wired Ethernet or Wi-Fi network. Review the target Windows build, edition, and language, and then confirm the data loss warning before the rebuild begins. You can choose whether to remove files or remove and sanitize files prior to Windows reinstalling. To learn more, see Cloud rebuild. [Windows settings backup and restore] New! This update introduces a Restore Summary that appears after you restore a backup profile to a new device. The summary gives a clear overview of what was successfully restored, including Windows settings and the list of Microsoft Store apps. This improves transparency during device transitions and helps you validate your restore results and continue setup on your new device with confidence. For more information see, Windows settings backup and restore overview. [Adaptive hibernate policy] New! This update improves the adaptive hibernate policy to provide more instant-on resumes from Modern Standby while helping preserve battery life when the charge is low. Noticeable changes include less hibernation while the battery is above 80% and hibernating sooner when the battery is below 10%. [Security] New! This update expands memory integrity protection across eligible devices. Supported PCs may now have memory integrity (HVCI) enabled during updates to help improve security and prepare devices for advanced Windows security features, while respecting existing user or IT administrator choices. For more information, see Expanding memory integrity protection across Windows devices. [Windows IPv6 networking support] New! Windows now supports IPv6 CLAT for Wi-Fi and Ethernet network interfaces, adding client-side 464XLAT translation so IPv4-only applications can continue reaching IPv4 services from IPv6-only networks. This helps organizations advance IPv6-only deployments while preserving compatibility for legacy IPv4 application scenarios. Prefix discovery: PREF64 is discovered through Router Advertisements (RA) by default, with DNS ipv4only.arpa available as a fallback. Requirements: CLAT requires SLAAC-based IPv6 addressing. DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation and Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) are not currently supported. Configuration: Enable CLAT by using netsh interface clat set global permit=enabled pref64fromdns=enabled pref64fromra=enabled or Group Policy under Network > TCPIP Settings > IPv6 Transition Technologies. [Data Protection API (DPAPI)] New! This update adds a warning before prompt-based protect and unprotect operations. The warning explains that this prompt-based experience will be retired in April 2027. If you or an app use these prompts, stop creating new prompt-protected data, use a supported non-interactive protection flow, and decrypt or migrate existing prompt-protected data before retirement. DPAPI operations that do not use the prompt-based flow aren't affected. For more details, see CRYPTPROTECT_PROMPTSTRUCT structure (dpapi.h). [Windows Spotlight] This update makes underlying platform changes to generally improve Windows Spotlight reliability on the lock screen. [Unicode] This update provides Windows text shaping support for Unicode 17.0, helping Windows correctly display and shape newly encoded characters and scripts. Unicode 17.0 added 4,803 characters, including support for four newly encoded scripts: Beria Erfe, Sidetic, Tai Yo, and Tolong Siki. These updates help keep Windows text support current as the Unicode Standard evolves and improve support for languages and writing systems used by people around the world. Microsoft is not aware of any new issues with this month's Patch Tuesday, and it also patched a long-standing issue that broke USB audio on some PCs. 10bsrnt.text: AI infrastructure company Fireworks said cybercriminals stole billing information and AI-specific data during two breaches last month. Fireworks published an updated notice on Monday saying it hired Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 to investigate a data breach it initially discovered on October 6. The San Mateo-based company was founded in 2022 and has more than 10,000 customers, offering an array of AI systems and tools to companies. Investigators found that a well-known, financially motivated cybercriminal group launched the attack and stole account and billing information as well as secrets — confidential digital pieces of information that grant access to human users or apps and allow them to communicate or perform actions. Fireworks said the incident affected a “limited number of customer accounts” — all of whom were notified of the attack. Monday’s alert from Fireworks also notes that the company experienced another incident on October 23 where a third-party cloud provider that hosted their R&D machines was attacked by cybercriminals. “On October 24, the unauthorized third party used [the provider] to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact,” the company said. The hackers gained access to internal Fireworks data, billing information, invoices and payment history as well as datasets and other AI-related data. The customers that were impacted have been notified. Fireworks is working with Palo Alto Networks on hardening its security posture and revoking compromised credentials. Digital workspace company Notion released its own notice that some of its customers were impacted by the Fireworks breaches. The company said it was notified of the incident on November 2 and disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleting all data in the Fireworks system. “On November 6, Fireworks notified us that malicious actors may have accessed potential customer data. Our team immediately began another internal investigation,” the company said. “We used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights, and we used them as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product. The Insights feature has been disabled as we investigate this incident, and we are no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.” LLMJacking Fireworks said its breaches are part of a larger string of attacks recently spotlighted by incident responders at Google. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant published a blog last week about a tactic known as "LLMJacking” where hackers hijack an enterprise’s access to large language models. Mandiant said it has responded to multiple LLMJacking incidents in 2026 spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers while impacting “organizations in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors.” “Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours,” the researchers explained. “Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million before access was revoked.” GTIG said it has identified a "diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions globally" that are responsible for the attacks. The groups are also maturing — with some focusing on initial access before handing off to other groups that monetize and resell the unauthorized access to large language models. Multiple investigations showed the groups were primarily trying to steal tokens or credentials which allow threat actors to establish footholds into target organizations' infrastructure. “As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware,” GTIG said. “This operational specialization will sustain a growing illicit resale marketplace, allowing threat actors to rapidly siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected.” No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

f0yhjj.text: A critical authentication bypass vulnerability in Xen Orchestra is being actively exploited in attacks that could grant administrator privileges and allow takeover of XCP-ng virtualization hosts. Xen Orchestra is a web-based management platform developed by French software company Vates, used to manage XCP-ng virtualization environments, including virtual machines, hosts, and pools. The vulnerability, tracked as VSA-2026-062, affects Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance (XOA) and allows remote attackers with network access to the management interface to bypass authentication using a specially crafted cookie. A CVE identifier and CVSS score have not been assigned yet. According to a Vates security advisory, the flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication tokens sent through REST API requests. The flaw stems from how Xen Orchestra processes authentication cookies. By sending a specially crafted cookie (authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D) containing an empty JSON object ({}), attackers can trick the platform into retrieving an existing authentication token and logging them in as its owner, without requiring actual credentials. Once authenticated, attackers can retrieve "reusable login token IDs" through the /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens REST API endpoint, which can be used for further access. "An adversary can bypass authentication and perform actions with 'Admin' privilege. Xen Orchestra compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full XCP-ng node takeover as root," warns Vates. The company has released Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 (stable) and 6.10.0 (latest), including patched xo-server packages 5.211.2 and 5.213.1 to fix these security vulnerabilities. Administrators should install the update immediately, and if not possible, restrict Xen Orchestra access to dedicated management networks and block known malicious IP addresses. Security researchers Filip Magic and Christoffer Olsen of TDC NET Security discovered the vulnerability. Exploited in attacks Vates confirmed that the vulnerability is being actively exploited and shared the following indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help administrators identify attacks: Attacker's infrastructure: Connections to 91.211.251.112:8001 or ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid.onion:3333. Suspicious authentication cookies: HTTP requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}. Virtual machines: A VM named pivot2. Modified VM configurations: Virtual machines configured with the hvm_serial: file parameter. Unusual files: /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar, /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar2, /.ustar5, and /.ustar6. Administrators can also run the following commands on XCP-ng hosts to check for unusual VM configurations, virtual machines configured to use a file for its serial port, and malicious files: xe vm-list params=name-label,platform | grep -B1 'hvm_serial: file' zgrep -- '-serial file:' /var/log/xensource.log* ls -la /etc/ld.so.preload /.ustar* /etc/cron.d/zz-ustar* However, Vates warns that exploitation will not generate any identifiers in logs, such as the use of specially crafted cookies, and instead must be detected through HTTP monitoring. The company also says these IOCs are only associated with this known attack campaign and may differ for other threat actors. Companies that believe they are compromised should rotate passwords and secrets used by their virtualization environments. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. rl9hpq.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an attack that exploited two now-patched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS to deliver a Python-based implant. The activity, observed by Huntress in early October 2026, involves the exploitation of a chain comprising CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. Patches for the two vulnerabilities were released by Ahsay Backup in mid-October 2026. The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach to deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners on compromised systems. "However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups," Huntress researcher Jonathan Semon said. Specifically, the unknown threat actor is said to have left five families of Jakarta Server Pages (JSP, formerly JavaServer Pages) web shells - nsmind.jsp, a signed API with command execution and file transfer capabilities using exec, cd, upload, and download parameters AhsayCBS.jsp, a loader that hides encrypted payloads in the pixel data of PNG images and runs them from memory Keyed command shell, which compares a hard-coded key against its own copy and, if it matches, runs the command via "cmd.exe" Keyed shell with file write, which expands on the keyed command web shell with the ability to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and deploy more tools status_<six_random_letters>.jsp or st_<six_random_letters>.jsp (e.g., st_jgaejj.jsp), which are used to run commands, recursively delete any path provided as input, and delete themselves using cmd, del, and rm parameters. "[AhsayCBS.jsp's] disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint," Huntress explained. "The web shell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later." The attack, besides deploying an XMRig miner masquerading as Microsoft Edge, has been found to deliver a second XMRig miner ("kvm-agent.exe") that restarts every minute through a SYSTEM scheduled task, while using a different wallet and mining pool. The most notable aspect of the intrusion revolves around the Python backdoor ("main.py"), which is designed to run only on the host it's staged on and prevent it from executing within a sandbox or an analyst's machine. It achieves this by computing the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file with the same name in the same directory housing the Python implant, and then runs an embedded x64 DLL in memory that contacts a command-and-control (C2) server ("creepexplosiondarknight[.]com"). In an attempt to fly under the radar, the attack chain also configures Microsoft Defender exclusions, while serving tunneling tools (GOST and Chisel) and legitimate remote access software (AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop) to establish persistent access. Evidence indicates that the threat actor may have targeted servers holding or managing backups. "On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI," Semon said. "Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident."

1pipa5y.text: The threat actor known as Blind Eagle has resurfaced with a new campaign targeting organizations in Latin America through judicial and administrative-themed phishing lures to deliver a remote access trojan (RAT) that shares its lineage with AsyncRAT and DCRat. "The campaign uses Portuguese and Spanish lures that resemble court notifications, fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents," Zenox said in a report shared with The Hacker News. Assessed to be a Spanish-speaking group and active since 2018, Blind Eagle (aka APT-C-36) has a track record of using spear-phishing lures to distribute commodity RATs like AsyncRAT, BitRAT, Lime RAT, NjRAT, Quasar RAT, and Remcos RAT. Attack chains begin with phishing emails targeting individuals who handle cases, contracts, judicial, or institutional service requests to trick them into opening a malware-laced attachment. One email containing a Colombian judicial-themed XHTML file has been identified as a weaponized Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) image that renders a bogus web page impersonating Colombia's Fiscalía General de la Nación, also referred to as the Office of the Attorney General. The web page, for its part, employs a technique known as HTML smuggling to assemble the next-stage ZIP archive payload locally in the web browser using ZipCrypto, thereby circumventing email security controls. Present within the ZIP archive is a JavaScript dropper that masquerades as Network Configuration Auditor version 2.7.298. The JavaScript code conducts environment reconnaissance, and collects details such as system version, network profile, installation date, memory size, computer name, environment variables, and directories localized in Portuguese and Spanish. Upon execution, it launches a Visual Basic Script that performs Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) and Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) bypass, while displaying a fake criminal-citation page as a distraction mechanism. In parallel, the malware also takes steps to delete the original XHTML artifact, clears Mark of the Web (MotW) metadata, and sets up persistence on the host under the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically executed on system startup. The attack culminates with the use of PowerShell to decode and launch the final RAT payload in memory. The trojan is an AsyncRAT fork with DCRat lineage based on code structure, configuration, build characteristics, and observed behavior. "The targeting of judicial, fiscal, administrative and educational organizations gives the operation access to highly sensitive legal, financial and institutional information," Zenox said. "Combined with the Portuguese and Spanish lures, Brazilian infrastructure, operational timezone and regional victimology, these elements establish the campaign as an APT-C-36 operation conducted through a Brazilian operational cluster." Zenox told The Hacker News that it could not confirm whether any of these attacks had succeeded against real-world targets. However, during the campaign period between late October and early November 2026, it observed a large-scale wave of targeted phishing involving nearly 3,300 malicious emails. While not all of these messages targeted organizations in Colombia, the country continues to remain a priority target for Blind Eagle for a combination of reasons. "The repeated targeting of Colombia likely reflects multiple factors, with one of the main enabling factors being the structural vulnerabilities and uneven security maturity across parts of the country's critical, public, financial, and private-sector infrastructure," Zenox security researcher Gabriel Alves said. "These conditions may increase the likelihood of successful compromises and offer greater opportunities to monetize access, steal sensitive data or funds, or reuse compromised credentials against critical systems. This is further supported by regional actors' familiarity with the Colombian context and is consistent with patterns observed among Latin American threat actors." (The story was updated after publication to include additional insights from Zenox.)

12grlaa.text: Cybercriminals are infecting devices on a large scale with spyware, increasingly compromising systems belonging to average people, according to a new report from the threat hunting firm iVerify. The company found a rate of 1.07 spyware infections per 1,000 consumer scans of the startup’s free online checks. The security firm reported a lower rate of infections for enterprises, detecting .7 infections per 1,000 scans, a disparity iVerify attributed to enterprises’ enforced patching, on-device detection and network security controls. Company co-founder Rocky Cole declined to say exactly how many consumer devices the firm tested, but said hundreds of thousands were scanned. An average Fortune 500 company experiences about 65 infections per year on its devices, he said. Notably, a large number of enterprise employees found with infected devices were rank and file workers as opposed to top executives. “The takeaway is that this is the year that iOS spyware went mainstream and became everyone's problem,” Cole said. “The number one threat actor using spyware targeting iPhones these days is not governments; it's just cyber criminals, and it's a problem that is indiscriminate.” Many of the device infections iVerify detected were used for credential and crypto theft as opposed to the more politically driven abuses often seen when advanced commercial spyware is deployed. Attacks were carried out by bad actors using leaked iOS exploit toolkits to “work at scale, delivering attacks through online ads, reaching ordinary employees, and erasing their traces before defenders could respond,” according to the iVerify report. About 75% of detections involved criminal actors deploying Coruna or DarkSword exploit kits, the report said. The other 25% were infected by mercenary spyware such as Pegasus. DarkSword is an advanced, full-chain JavaScript-based iOS exploit kit and spyware framework first made public in March. Deployed as a “watering hole” attack, DarkSword allows users to be infected without clicking on a link. Simply visiting a compromised website through a web browser can trigger the attack. Coruna is also delivered via web-based attacks, where people visiting malicious sites trigger WebKit and kernel vulnerabilities. The spyware framework was purloined from a defense contractor and has been used by cybercriminals to facilitate the theft of cryptocurrency from over 42,000 iOS devices using fake Chinese-language financial websites. The Google Threat Intelligence Group first discovered the Coruna exploit kit in February 2025 and it slowly proliferated across last year. It has been directly tied to the actions of a former L3Harris Trenchant executive who pleaded guilty to stealing exploits and selling them on the black market in exchange for crypto payments. The executive, Peter Williams, was sentenced to seven years in prison in February 2026. As with DarkSword, iVerify’s report said, Coruna is part of a “broader trend where mobile exploit frameworks… have shifted from rare, highly restricted intelligence operations into wider circulation.” Owners of the devices infected with DarkSword and Coruna did not receive Apple threat notifications, the report said. Both exploit frameworks offer the same level of phone takeover as advanced commercial spyware brands like the zero-click Pegasus exploits and can expose messages, photos, emails and turn on microphones and cameras. The difference is that a broad population can access DarkSword and Coruna, whereas Pegasus and other commercial brands are exclusively sold to nation-state clients. “One in 900 is a dragnet number, not a targeting number,” Nic Adams, co-founder and CEO of cyberkinetics company 0rcus said about the survey’s infection rate. “Mercenary spyware was built as a scalpel — now it’s being used as a net.” Android is confronting a similar shift, the report said, as a large supply of inexpensive and turnkey spyware kits are letting bad actors easily take over phones from afar. “The primary goal of these attacks isn't to steal intellectual property or get a leg up in trade negotiations — it's just cybercrime. Every single employee and every single person is potentially at risk,” Cole said. The firm’s researchers had expected to find a decline in the rate of detected spyware infections this year since the number of average consumers using the free device checks quadrupled, Cole said. Two years ago, many of the people getting their devices checked were elites with reasons to suspect potential spyware. An iVerify report published in December 2024 found Pegasus infections on 2.5 per 1,000 devices scanned. Coruna and DarkSword were not in the marketplace at the time and nation-state sponsored attacks using advanced commercial spyware were seen as by far the predominant threat. . “Businesses need to update their threat models to stop focusing on VIPs and just assume this is a problem that everyone in the organization has to tackle,” Cole said. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

1w8hdky.text: Today is Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday, with security updates addressing a record-breaking 1,235 flaws, including one actively exploited Microsoft Outlook zero-day vulnerability.This Patch Tuesday addresses 66 "Critical" vulnerabilities, 48 of which are Remote Code Execution (RCE), 15 are Elevation of Privilege (EoP), and three are Use-After-Free in Microsoft Edge.Of the 1,235 vulnerabilities, approximately 639 are categorized under Windows or Microsoft Windows products/components.When BleepingComputer reports on Patch Tuesday security updates, we only count vulnerabilities released by Microsoft on Patch Tuesday itself.Therefore, today's total excludes 108 flaws fixed earlier this month, including one Entra Device Registration, 82 Mariner, and 25 Microsoft Edge flaws.November's Patch Tuesday comes after a record-breaking 1,411 flaws in the October updates as Microsoft continues to use AI to find and patch vulnerabilities.This month's Patch Tuesday fixes one zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook that was exploited in attacks.Microsoft classifies a zero-day flaw as publicly disclosed or actively exploited when no official fix is available.The actively exploited zero-day vulnerability addressed in the November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates is:Microsoft patched a Microsoft Outlook Spoofing zero-day vulnerability that was actively exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes."An unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it in an affected version of Microsoft Outlook," warns Microsoft."Opening the file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. Exploitation requires network connectivity and user interaction."This type of vulnerability is known as an NTLM credential disclosure flaw, where a malicious attachment, when opened, causes Windows to connect to an attacker-controlled network share.When connecting, Windows may automatically attempt to authenticate to the remote server, exposing the user's NTLMv2 authentication hash, which can then be captured by the attacker and potentially cracked offline.The recovered credentials could then be used to gain unauthorized access to corporate accounts.Below is the complete list of resolved vulnerabilities in the November 2026 updates. Note, this report does include the flaws fixed earlier this month.To access the full description of each vulnerability and the systems it affects, you can view the full report here. 2gskgi.text: Fireworks AI disclosed on Monday that its investigation into a security incident first reported early last month uncovered further malicious activity, affecting account and billing information, alongside secrets, datasets, and incomplete models for a "limited set of accounts." In a notice published on October 10, 2026, the company said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT. At that time, the AI infrastructure provider said it only found evidence that environment variables, including API keys and tokens stored as secrets, were captured in certain affected accounts, adding that there were no signs that customer models, datasets, training data, inference traffic, or personal information were accessed. In response to the incident, Fireworks AI took the step of revoking the compromised internal credentials and rotating service account tokens, along with affected Fireworks API keys and keys created by the threat actor. The latest bulletin from the company reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously thought. The company said attackers reached its development environment via an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development (R&D) machines on October 23, 2026. "On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," it added. "As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use." The breach is said to have provided access to the following types of information - Resource metadata: Fireworks resource identifiers, display names, descriptions, and creation time Billing information: billing and shipping addresses, invoice and payment history, account balance, and credit usage Model weights and datasets: a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets for certain customers Fireworks AI said payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not impacted by the security incident. It also said it's alerting customers whose data was impacted. The company also noted that it has implemented security hardening procedures, such as credential revocation and rotation; isolating affected systems to prevent further unauthorized activity and lateral movement; tightening access controls; and improving its logging and monitoring systems. "The evidence indicates links to a cybercriminal threat actor group, which is financially motivated and aimed at selling tokens from unauthorized access to large language models (LLMs) to illicit routing gateways," it said. The activity is assessed to be part of an emerging threat known as LLMjacking, which refers to the act of hijacking a victim's LLM through stolen credentials to fuel a criminal enterprise that thrives on peddling the access to other threat actors, while leaving the legitimate owner to pay the bill. Last week, Google issued a warning that threat actors are increasingly targeting AI infrastructure for LLMjacking in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors. Notion Impacted by Fireworks AI Incident Popular productivity and note-taking application Notion has disclosed that the security incident targeting Fireworks AI impacted "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces." In a post shared on Reddit, one user said: "looks like all of us are part of that <1%." While the initial assessment was that the breach allowed the threat actor to access Notion AI synthetic testing data, it has since come to light that it may also have involved potential customer data. "Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results." Notion has also emphasized that no other features across its platform were affected by the incident. The Insights feature has since been disabled as it continues to investigate the breach and the company is no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks. Affected customers are advised to review the impacted data securely inside their workspace. If those with affected workspaces have pasted sensitive information, passwords, API keys, or other credentials during the attack window, it's recommended to rotate them with immediate effect.

1efecbp.text: Binance is warning about a vulnerability in Apple’s iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 that could allow third-party apps to read private files stored by other apps, including cryptocurrency seed phrases, secret keys, and login credentials. The crypto exchange clarifies that the issue is at the iOS level and does not impact only the Binance app. “A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem,” Binance says. At this time, no cryptocurrency losses have been confirmed, but Binance urges users to install the update immediately as a precaution. The company recommends that users delete any unnecessary and untrusted apps and apply the latest versions for iOS and other apps. Where compromise is suspected, Binance advises users to transfer funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset all active login sessions. Public exploit available “worse_query” is a publicly disclosed iOS sandbox escape technique that allows an application to cross security boundaries and access the storage of other applications. Yesterday, a proof-of-concept exploit has been published that uses a tool called WQ Files to perform attacks relying on the technique. Specifically, WQ Files uses “worse_query” to browse, export, edit, and delete other apps’ data without requiring a jailbreak. An attacker could The tool must be installed on an iPhone for the attack to work, but an attacker could distribute it through untrusted sources as a sideloaded app, bypassing Apple's App Store. WQ Files has been confirmed to work on iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2, the same versions that Binance warned about. Apple on November 9 released iOS security updates (iOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3, and 18.7.12) that address nine flaws. One of the fixed vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-113963, could allow an app to access sensitive user data. It is unclear if this is the same security issue Binance is warning of, though. The CVE-2026-113963 problem was reported by László Várady flaw, who found that the access occurred through App Intents, not App Group containers. BleepingComputer has contacted Apple for clarifications and a request for comment, and we will add an update once we receive more details. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. srpx63.text: The ransomware attack is over. Your team has restored the client’s data, brought systems back online and put business operations back on track. From a technical standpoint, the recovery was a success. But the client still has questions. Why did updates go quiet for two days? What drove the recovery costs up? And where did the 31 hours of emergency labor on the invoice come from? Recovering from ransomware is only part of the job. Clients also need to know what happened, what recovery involved and what it cost them. When communication falls short or unexpected charges appear, even a technically successful recovery can leave clients questioning the value of their MSP relationship. The disruption may be behind them, but their doubts can carry into the next renewal conversation. The trend: Slow, fragmented recovery erodes trust and renewals Ransomware recovery can take days, even when teams have backups and a response plan in place. According to industry reports, only 16% of affected organizations fully recovered within a day. Over half (55%) recovered within a week. For businesses that depend on their systems to serve customers and generate revenue, every additional day of disruption carries a cost. The stakes extend to the MSP, too. Kaseya’s 2026 Cybersecurity Outlook report found that 12% of MSPs lost clients following security incidents, with ransomware, account takeover and business email compromise among the main reasons. When recovery involves delays, fragmented efforts or gaps in communication, clients struggle to understand what is happening and when they can expect normal operations to resume. They may also question unexpected costs or wonder whether their provider has the situation under control. Clients expect cyberattacks to happen, but they also expect their MSP to respond quickly, coordinate recovery and keep them informed. When those expectations go unmet, a technically successful recovery may still leave clients questioning whether they should renew their contracts. A successful recovery depends on both the technical response and the client experience. MSPs that set expectations early, communicate consistently and explain costs before they become surprises have a stronger chance of preserving client trust long after the systems come back online. Where your recovery process breaks down Most MSPs have skilled people. The trouble starts when those people work across disconnected tools in the middle of a crisis. Tool sprawl slows everyone down Backup, monitoring, ticketing and billing live in separate consoles. Your techs spend incident hours piecing together context instead of restoring systems. Handoffs break An alert fires in one tool, a ticket opens in another and a restore job runs in a third. Nothing links them, so no one can say what the attack touched or what’s still down. Billing falls through the cracks Emergency labor, restore time and after-hours work often go untracked. Someone reconstructs those hours from memory days later. You either lose margin or send an invoice the client doesn’t recognize, and you do it at the worst possible time. Client updates depend on who’s free Without a single ticket trail, communication comes down to whoever has a spare minute. Some clients get a call every few hours. Others hear nothing until the work is done. Each of these problems looks small by itself. Together, they turn a recoverable incident into a trust problem. 5 signs your recovery process is costing you client trust Clients chase you for updates. They have to ask what’s happening instead of hearing from your team. Your team scrambles across tools. Technicians waste valuable recovery time piecing together information from disconnected systems. No one owns the full picture. Handoffs leave gaps in who knows what’s restored, what’s still down and what needs attention. Recovery bills come as a surprise. Emergency labor and after-hours work appear on invoices without clear explanations. Recovery ends without clear answers. Clients are left unsure what happened, what it cost or what you’ll do to prevent a repeat. What good recovery looks like for an MSP Strong recovery runs on one timeline and one source of truth. Everyone on your team sees the same facts, so your client hears the same story no matter who calls. Updates go out on a schedule you set, before the client asks. When the incident closes, the invoice matches the work, because your team logged the work as it happened. Track three numbers to see how you’re doing: Time to first client update: How long after detection does the client hear from you? Time to restore: How long until their critical systems run again? Time to invoice: How fast can you send an accurate bill after closing the incident? If any of these takes too long, you have a process gap that clients will notice. Closing those gaps takes more than working harder during an incident. It takes tools that share data from the start. The fix: Unifying RMM, PSA and BCDR with Kaseya Trifecta The 2026 Kaseya Cybersecurity Report found that two factors supported faster incident recovery: well-trained internal IT or security teams (35%) and integrated security and IT management tools (18%). Kaseya Trifecta puts RMM, PSA and BCDR in one connected platform. The idea is simple. When your monitoring, ticketing and recovery tools share a workflow, your team stops stitching context together and starts fixing the problem. Here’s how it maps to the breakdowns above: Fragmented context: RMM, PSA and BCDR run on one workflow and one data set, so your techs see the full picture in one place. Slow handoffs: Recovery events tie directly to tickets and endpoints. You know what’s affected and what’s restored without chasing updates. Billing blind spots: Time and labor land in the ticket as the work happens, then flow to billing. Your invoice reflects what your team did. Inconsistent updates: One auditable incident record gives every team member the same facts. Your client gets consistent communication, whoever is on shift. This matches what the report found. Teams that recover quickly pair skilled people with tools that connect. Trifecta gives your people that connection. Keep the client, not just the data Surviving the attack is the baseline. Your clients expect it. What they remember is whether recovery felt organized, transparent and fair. Faster resolution gives you the foundation for all of that. It shortens downtime, makes your updates credible and keeps your invoices accurate. Those benefits help protect renewals long after the incident closes. Want to see how MSPs cut resolution times?
