7nsibn.text: President Donald Trump has nominated the chief information security officer of Palantir to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, potentially marking a turning point for an organization that has endured massive staff cuts and years of Republican attacks. The president selected Michael LoSapio on Monday as the next head of the top civilian cyber defense agency, which has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since Trump returned to the Oval Office. A previous nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew from consideration earlier this year after spending months in limbo on Capitol Hill; Nick Andersen has led CISA in an acting capacity since February. The Homeland Security Department’s cyber wing lost more than 1,000 personnel — one-third of its workforce — and has seen its budget slashed by billions during the second Trump administration, following years of GOP complaints that its efforts to combat online disinformation during elections singled out conservative voices and infringed upon free speech rights. As a result, CISA remained largely behind the scenes ahead of last week’s midterm elections. However, a spokesperson said the organization “provided voluntary, no-cost services” like vulnerability scanning ahead of Election Day and activated its Incident Coordination Group to serve as a threat information sharing hub. It is unclear if the Senate will take up LoSapio’s nomination during the already jam-packed lame duck session of Congress, with lawmakers looking to approve a must-pass government funding measure and the annual defense policy bill, among other priorities. Should lawmakers adjourn next month without approving his nomination, Trump would have to nominate LoSapio again next year for consideration by the incoming Democratic majority. A spokesperson for Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY), the chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Sen. Gary Peters (MI), the panel’s top Democrat, said in a statement that CISA “needs a steady hand at the wheel who is committed to rebuilding its capabilities, supporting its workforce, and ensuring it can effectively support critical infrastructure operators navigate evolving threats.” LoSapio must “demonstrate that he possesses the independent judgment and qualifications to decisively place national security and the national interest above political pressure,” added Peters, who is retiring in January. If the nomination is resubmitted next year, LoSapio could face increased scrutiny due to his role at Palantir, a software and artificial intelligence company with ties to the Trump administration. LoSapio joined the firm in 2017, leading its infrastructure and network security group before becoming CIO in late 2024, according to his LinkedIn profile. Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS), who is expected to retake the reins of the House Homeland Security Committee, has signaled he plans to conduct thorough oversight of all DHS components, including CISA. Andersen is widely seen as an effective leader and is well-liked. His temporary term expired September 24 based on federal statute limiting how long acting directors can stay in place. He remained on the job afterward through a bureaucratic move. By nominating LoSapio, the administration starts the clock again. A former government cybersecurity official said via text that it is hard to know what to make of the LoSapio selection, “with the nomination coming out right at the beginning of the lame duck and exactly at the same time as Nick Andersen needed this to happen in order to remain Acting Director.” LoSapio’s name had been floated several months ago, the former official said, but he questioned whether the administration would really push for him to be confirmed in 2026 and stick with him in 2027. Other AI and cybersecurity experts said that while LoSapio’s background at Palantir gives him a unique perspective at a time when AI is becoming increasingly embedded in national security and every day cyber operations, that perspective isn’t sufficient for running CISA. “There’s a big difference between securing a company that builds AI-powered technology and understanding how to defend against AI-driven threats” and running CISA, said Chris Cochran, who is vice president of AI Security at the SANS Institute. “What I’ll be watching for is whether he can bridge that gap, particularly as we move toward autonomous attacks, AI agents, and adversaries operating at machine speed.” Editor's Note: Updated 3:10 p.m. Eastern time with comments from Sen. Gary Peters (D-MI). Updated 12:15 p.m. with comments from experts. No previous articleNo new articlesMartin Matishakis the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.Suzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

1afase9.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 10, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security An iOS sandbox escape published on GitHub lets an app read other apps' files on iPhones running iOS 26 and 27. That puts seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk of exposure to malicious apps, Binance warned today. Apple's updates for iOS 26 and 27, released yesterday, do not list a fix. A researcher who goes by forcequit, in collaboration with 0xjohnny, released the escape, called worse_query, on Sunday, a day before those updates came out. Neither the exchange nor the researcher reported any attacks or thefts involving it. The exchange told users to delete apps installed from untrusted sources, such as sideloaded or manually signed apps, and to update iOS and all their apps. No fix for the escape has been confirmed. For anyone who suspects a breach, the exchange's security warning advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and resetting all active login sessions. The researcher's proof-of-concept code can reach every app's data container on an iPhone, and some system folders on iOS 27. To use it, an app has to set up an App Group container. He says the code is for developers and "isn't useful by itself." Other developers have built apps on it that people can install. One of them is WQ Files, a file manager that developer Christoph Kolbicz built on worse_query. It reaches other apps' data without a jailbreak or a kernel exploit, and it can edit, delete and clear that data. WQ Files installs via sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the App Group it needs when used with an Apple ID. No one involved has said whether an app from the App Store could use worse_query. The three versions in the exchange's warning are the ones listed as tested in the WQ Files release notes. The researcher gives a wider range. Of these sources, only Erosion's developers list iOS 27.2.1, which came out yesterday, and none lists iOS 26.7.3. They added 27.2.1 this week in a README change with the note "pretty sure 27.2.1 is supported". Yesterday's updates, iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3, fixed two iMessage flaws and several Bluetooth bugs. The security notes for iOS 27.2.1 do not mention worse_query or any sandbox issues, nor do the iOS 26.7.3 notes. Apple does not disclose, discuss, or confirm security issues until it has investigated and a patch or release is available, the notes say. In a reply on X, the researcher wrote that he had not planned to release worse_query early. He added that "Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here." The exchange did not name any wallet app as exposed, and neither did the researcher nor the developers of the apps built on worse_query.

1vg0ckr.text: Russian state-linked hackers compromised government email servers in Romania and Kazakhstan using new malware to secretly intercept messages, including emails exchanged with NATO and European Union officials, according to research published Tuesday. Slovak cybersecurity firm ESET attributed the campaign to Turla, a long-running Russian espionage group linked to the country's Federal Security Service (FSB). The hackers used a previously unknown toolkit dubbed Cereal to monitor email traffic, steal specific messages and maintain access to compromised Microsoft Exchange servers without being detected. “The Cereal toolset is a carefully constructed instrument for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage. It leaves little on disk, avoids external infrastructure that could be discovered and blocked, and conceals itself within legitimate Exchange processes,” ESET said. The researchers said they first discovered the toolkit in November 2025 on a government email server in Kazakhstan and later identified it at a Romanian government organization. In Romania, the malware was configured to collect emails exchanged with NATO and EU institutions. The attack came amid rising tensions between Russia and NATO over the war in Ukraine, including repeated incidents involving Russian drones entering or approaching Romanian territory. In Kazakhstan, ESET said the intrusion took place amid growing scrutiny of Russian exiles and Kremlin critics living in the country. However, researchers could not determine whether the hackers were specifically seeking information about dissidents. The campaign stands out for its unusual approach to concealing the hackers' activities, researchers said. Rather than relying on separate servers to control the malware, the attackers used the victims' own compromised Exchange servers to issue commands and manage the operation. This allowed the hackers to operate without relying on external servers that security researchers could detect, block or shut down. "Abusing a compromised Exchange server as a central operational hub is a rare technique, used by only a handful of APT groups," ESET said. "Turla has used variations of this approach in the past." One component of Turla's new toolkit, called CerealBox, was embedded directly into a Microsoft Exchange service responsible for processing email traffic. It allowed the attackers to identify and capture messages of interest as they passed through the server. According to ESET, the technique has not previously been documented in other malware families and demonstrates the attackers' detailed knowledge of Microsoft's email infrastructure. The researchers could not determine how the attackers initially gained access to the government servers or how much information they obtained. Also known as Secret Blizzard and Venomous Bear, Turla has operated since at least 2004 and is considered one of Russia's most established state-linked hacking groups. The group has a long history of targeting government agencies, diplomatic missions and defense organizations across Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East. According to ESET, roughly 70% of the countries targeted by Turla since 2022 have been former Soviet republics or European countries with historical ties to the Soviet Union. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

563jov.text: SAP patched 35 vulnerabilities in its November 2026 security updates, including four maximum-severity issues affecting its NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, and Gateway software. The company addressed memory corruption (CVE-2026-76964) and missing authentication (CVE-2026-120017) flaws in the NetWeaver Application Server ABAP's Internet Communication Manager and SAML2 Service Provider components. NetWeaver is the core app platform that underpins SAP's business software and handles application integration, authentication, user management, and data processing. The other two maximum severity vulnerabilities stem from a broken access control weakness (CVE-2026-89103) in SAP Gateway and a memory corruption issue (CVE-2026-89126) in SAP Web Dispatcher. Gateway is a core framework that enables external apps to securely connect to SAP backend systems, while Web Dispatcher (deployed in almost every enterprise SAP environment) is a specialized component that acts as a load balancer and reverse proxy for web requests entering an SAP system architecture. Cybersecurity firm Onapsis, which found and reported three of these security issues, collectively tracks CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126 as ICM2SHELL and the CVE-2026-89103 pre-auth remote code execution vulnerability as PROXYGATE. "ICM2SHELL turns a routine part of web traffic into a point of ingress for attackers. [..] The result is remote code execution against the component that faces the network by design: no SAP user, no password and no user interaction," Onapsis said. "PROXYGATE works by convincing the SAP Gateway that an unauthenticated, external attacker is one of the internal application servers. [..] There is no SAP user, no password, and no user interaction, yet full control of the SAP system as the account that owns the installation is achieved. On a production ERP system, that means direct exposure of the business data, transaction integrity, and the availability of critical business applications." SAP rated these four vulnerabilities 10/10 on the CVSS severity scale, stating that unauthenticated attackers can exploit them to fully compromise the targeted systems remotely. More recently patched max severity SAP security issues These are the latest in a string of other maximum-severity flaws SAP has fixed in multiple components in recent months. For instance, it patched CVE-2026-58231 in the Commerce Cloud cloud-based e-commerce platform in August, which threat intelligence firm Defused flagged as actively exploited in attacks days after the patch. It also addressed two more max severity flaws in September and October: a memory corruption flaw in the SAP Kernel code (tracked as CVE-2026-44756 and dubbed OVERPASS by Onapsis security researchers who reported it) and an OAuth2 SSRF vulnerability affecting multi-tenant BTP applications (CVE-2026-89111). The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 14 SAP security flaws as actively exploited since November 2021, three of which ransomware groups also abused in the wild. SAP is a German multinational software company that reported revenues exceeding €36 billion in fiscal year 2025 and serves 99 of the 100 largest companies worldwide.
